sources.title: Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you
passages: Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop.
Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more.
As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining.

Trip-planning and saved list search is rolling out to the more than 200 countries where Ask Maps is available, while “know before you go” tips and appointment-finding are launching in the US to start.

extraction.body: Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days. As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. From there, Ask Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with a list of stops, while also showing your route and numbered pins for each location on the map. You can share the itinerary with friends or family members, as well as export it to Google Docs on desktop. [Video: Ask Maps trip planning] You can ask Maps to show your trip schedule before you leave, or select the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more. You can also view “know before you go” details about parking, car charging, weather conditions, potential delays, and tolls during your trip. In addition to trip planning, you can now use Ask Maps to find specific beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, and have it call the locations for you. You can also use Ask Maps to find saved places on your list by asking something like, “Which spots on saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” [Video: Ask Maps "know before you go"] Google is expanding Ask Maps to over 30 countries in Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Trip-planning and saved list search is rolling out to the more than 200 countries where Ask Maps is available, while “know before you go” tips and appointment-finding are launching in the US to start.

extraction.body: Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users. The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day. Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions. For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop. When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop. Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses. The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf. Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

extraction.body: Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users. The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day. Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions. For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop. When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop. Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses. The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf. Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

Read more › Health Secretary Testifies: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary and longtime vaccine skeptic, told a Senate committee on Wednesday that his department had advised that “every child” get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine — a stark contrast with his past remarks. Mr. Kennedy has previously called the vaccine a “personal choice.” Read more › Navy Secretary John Phelan was fired on Wednesday after months of infighting with senior Pentagon leaders and disagreements over how to revive the Navy’s struggling shipbuilding program. Mr. Phelan is leaving the Pentagon and the Trump administration effective immediately, wrote Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, in a terse statement. In his role leading the Navy, Mr. Phelan had championed the “Golden Fleet,” a major investment in new ships including a “Trump-class” battleship. But Mr. Phelan’s leadership was marred by feuds with senior leaders in the Pentagon, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg, Pentagon and congressional officials said. Mr. Phelan is the first service secretary to leave the administration, though he is the second one to clash with the defense secretary. Mr. Hegseth also has butted heads with Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll over promotions and a host of other issues. Mr. Hegseth fired the Army’s chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, earlier this month. The Navy secretary has no role overseeing deployed forces, and Mr. Phelan’s firing is not likely to have significant implications for the conduct of the Iran war or U.S. Navy operations to blockade Iranian ports or open the Strait of Hormuz. As the Navy’s top civilian leader, his main responsibility is to oversee the building of the future naval and Marine Corps force. Mr. Feinberg, in particular, had grown increasingly dissatisfied with Mr. Phelan’s handling of the Navy’s major new shipbuilding initiative, and had been siphoning off responsibility for the project from him, said the congressional official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters. Mr. Phelan, a White House appointee, also had a contentious relationship with his deputy, Under Secretary Hung Cao, who is more aligned with Mr. Hegseth, especially on some of the social and cultural battles that have defined the defense secretary’s tenure, the officials said. A senior administration official said that Mr. Hegseth informed Mr. Phelan before the Pentagon’s official announcement that he and President Trump had decided that the Navy needed new leadership. Still, the timing of Mr. Phelan’s firing caught some Pentagon and congressional officials off guard. On Wednesday, Mr. Phelan was making the rounds on Capitol Hill, talking to senators about his upcoming annual hearing with lawmakers to discuss the Navy’s budget request and other priorities. “Secretary Phelan’s abrupt dismissal is troubling,” Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said in a statement Wednesday night. “In the midst of President Trump’s war of choice in Iran, at a moment when our naval forces are stretched thin across multiple theaters, this kind of disruption at the top sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines, to our allies, and to our adversaries.” Mr. Phelan also had a close relationship with Mr. Trump. In December, Mr. Phelan appeared alongside Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort to announce the “Golden Fleet” and the new class of battleships bearing Mr. Trump’s name. Bryan Clark, a naval analyst at the Hudson Institute, said that Mr. Phelan was “driving the Navy in a different direction” than what Mr. Hegseth and Mr. Feinberg wanted. “He was championing initiatives like the battleship and frigate that don’t align with where the D.O.W. leadership is taking the military, which is toward submarines, stealth aircraft, unmanned systems and software-driven capabilities like electronic warfare and cyber,” Mr. Clark said in an email, using the abbreviation for Department of War, as the administration calls the Defense Department. Mr. Phelan also clashed with Mr. Hegseth over personnel issues in the Navy and Marine Corps, a former senior military official said. Mr. Hegseth has directed service secretaries to scrub the social media accounts of general- and admiral-level promotion candidates to ensure they are not deemed too “woke” by Mr. Hegseth’s standards, the official said. “The White House is clearly upset because his stance is not popular,” Dr. Emanuel said. “but he has not fundamentally moved his stance on vaccines.” Indeed, Mr. Kennedy also insisted that hygiene and sanitation — and not vaccination — were responsible for the drop in deaths from infectious diseases during the 20th century, citing a 2000 study as proof. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the Republican chairman of the Health Committee who is also a physician and has tangled repeatedly with Mr. Kennedy on vaccines, pushed back, telling the secretary he had cited the study out of context. Mr. Cassidy, who voted to confirm Mr. Kennedy only reluctantly — and only after the secretary made a series of promises to secure the senator’s vote — seemed irritated by Mr. Kennedy’s emphasis on chronic disease over infectious disease. Mr. Kennedy noted that three Americans died of measles over the past decade, while roughly two million die from chronic disease each year. But after the hearing, Mr. Cassidy lamented the measles deaths, saying there should be a focus on infectious disease. “We are a first-world country, and speaking as a physician that knows this can be prevented, it grieves me,” he said. “It grieves me.” The senator himself is walking a fine line. He is facing a tough primary election next month; Mr. Trump has endorsed his challenger, as has the Make America Healthy Again PAC, which is aligned with Mr. Kennedy. Asked by a reporter whether the secretary had lived up to the promises he made, Mr. Cassidy declined to answer. “We’ll talk later,” he said. During the hearings, which began in the House last Thursday, Mr. Kennedy revealed that after firing or laying off close to 20,000 employees at the Department of Health and Human Services last year, he was now hiring 12,000 new workers to replace them. He told lawmakers on Tuesday that he needed to “make sure that we have people to do every job.” Mr. Kennedy told lawmakers he supported the nomination, but he refused to commit to accepting all of Dr. Schwartz’s decisions on vaccines. “I’m not going to make that kind of commitment,” he said on Tuesday. When Wednesday’s hearing was over, Mr. Cassidy offered an oblique assessment of the secretary’s performance. “Things were illuminating,” he said. After tangling with Kennedy over vaccines during the hearing, Senator Bill Cassidy, the chairman of the Senate Health Committee, had little to say about the secretary. “Things were illuminating,” Cassidy said when asked about Kennedy’s performance, and demurred when asked whether Kennedy has lived up to the promises he had made to persuade Cassidy to back his nomination last year. “We’ll talk later,” the senator said. While Kennedy once more backed away from his criticism of vaccines on Wednesday, Cassidy also offered a pointed defense of vaccines, and sounded angry over measles deaths: “We are a first world country, and speaking as a physician that knows this can be prevented, it grieves me,” he said. “It grieves me.” In remarks about artificial intelligence, the health secretary suggested it could ultimately replace the Food and Drug Administration. He made a puzzling statement about advances in veterinary medicine, saying he had been reading about a man whose dog had cancer. “His owner used A.I. to develop a personalized treatment that cured the cancer,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to see that now in medicine, across medicine, and we’re very excited about it.” It was not immediately clear to what the secretary was referring. The Food and Drug Administration, an agency of his department, performs careful reviews of veterinary medicine for safety and efficacy. “I’ve never seen a case where an article in the M.M.W.R. that got to that stage was not published,” said Dr. Michael Iademarco, who led the center that included the publication’s operations from 2014 to 2022. Andrew Nixon, a spokesman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said that “scientific reports are routinely reviewed at multiple levels to ensure they meet the highest standards before publication.” He said that assessment “identified concerns regarding the methodological approach to estimating vaccine effectiveness, and the manuscript was not accepted for publication.” The Secretary of the Navy, John Phelan, is leaving the Pentagon and the Trump administration effective immediately, Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, wrote in a terse statement. Phelan had been feuding for months with Undersecretary Hung Cao, according to Pentagon officials. Cao, who previously served in the Navy, will become Acting Secretary of the Navy, Parnell said. But Phelan’s sudden departure was not expected. In July, the agency issued a memo saying that a wide array of federal decisions and consultations on wind and solar projects that are typically carried out by career employees would be subject to new layers of review by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s office. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also issued new restrictions for renewable energy projects. Those actions brought federal permitting for many renewable energy projects to a standstill, developers have said. Career staffers were unsure how to move forward with once-routine work such as approving plans for access roads. Former Interior Department officials said it was unworkable for the secretary to review each of the hundreds of small decisions needed to approve projects, creating lengthy delays. While fewer than 5 percent of solar and wind projects are on lands directly overseen by the Interior Department, even developers that build on private land often need federal approvals. If, for instance, a solar or wind farm is going to disturb nearby wetlands, the developer may need a water permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which in turn often consults with the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service to gauge the effects on sensitive habitat. Many of the Afghans in Doha have told officials that they would not voluntarily agree to being sent to Congo, according to a person familiar with the planning, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe confidential discussions. Some Afghans questioned whether they would be protected there. Others asked why they would go to Congo when their loved ones are in the United States.

extraction.body: JPMorgan Chase said Monday it is working to resolve a technical issue that was impacting services, including transactions to other banks. The bank said in a statement it has "experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems -- there is no evidence this is cyber-related." "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," the statement continued. "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue." JPMorgan Chase said customers still have access to their accounts and funds. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today," it said. Amid the reports, U.S. Bank said that its systems are "not directly impacted" but that clients may experience transaction delays while trying to send or receive Zelle payments with another bank. passages: No data breaches or security issues were reported in connection with the outage.Chase's History of Technical ChallengesThis is not the first time Chase customers have faced app or online banking disruptions.

While not all customers experienced disruptions, the volume of complaints suggested a significant outage affecting a broad user base.Chase has not issued a formal statement detailing the cause, but sources familiar with the situation said technical teams were investigating potential server or network issues.

Reporting problems through the app's feedback tools helps the bank identify and address root causes.Chase's Response and Future OutlookThe bank typically issues updates via its official social media accounts and website during significant outages.

The bank has invested heavily in digital infrastructure, but scaling to serve tens of millions of users presents ongoing complexities.Industry analysts note that major banks like Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo periodically encounter outages due to high traffic, software updates or third-party dependencies.

The issues come at a time when mobile banking has become essential for millions of Americans handling daily finances.Users took to social media and customer service lines to voice frustration as the app displayed error messages, loading failures or complete inaccessibility.

Mobile banking usage has surged post-pandemic, increasing pressure on systems designed for growing demand.Chase has generally responded quickly to past issues, restoring service and communicating through social channels.

Banks and regulators collaborate on guidelines to enhance reliability and customer protection.While Saturday's Chase app issues caused temporary inconvenience, quick resolution and communication typically mitigate long-term effects.
NEW YORK — Chase Bank customers across the United States reported widespread problems with the Chase mobile app Saturday, with many unable to access accounts, view balances or complete transactions.

Others turned to alternative apps or called customer service, leading to longer wait times.Chase's customer support channels experienced increased volume, with some users waiting extended periods for assistance.
Enabling notifications for account activity and reviewing statements regularly can help spot issues early.The incident may prompt Chase to accelerate upgrades or redundancies.

Customers at banks including Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo said they experienced outages coast to coast on Monday — days after technical snafus wreaked havoc for flight passengers and Microsoft customers. There were nearly 5,000 reports of outages at Chase and about 1,400 between BofA and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com . JPMorgan Chase said a software bug in systems it runs in-house slowed service for some customers – and may have affected other banks. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” JPMorgan said in a statement. It added that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds.” The nation’s largest bank said other lenders may have been affected when JPMorgan was a party to a transaction with them, but that “this is not a systemic issue.” In other words, reported outages at other banks appeared to be due to customers trying to do business with Chase accounts. JPMorgan said it was working to resolve the problem by the end of the day. Customers reported issues at Capital One, PNC, US Bank and the Zelle money transfer app. Zelle indicated any problems customers faced sending payments were due to problems at partner banks. “Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should. Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds,” a Zelle spokesperson told The Post. Capital One made a similar statement, suggesting it was indirectly affected by banking woes at Chase. “Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” a Capital One spokesperson said. Some customers said online they couldn’t use their banking apps. “My Chase App has a warning that I’ve never seen before: Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later,” one user wrote on Reddit. Earlier in the day, Chase said it was sorry to an X user complaining of banking woes. “I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We’re sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience,” a Chase support account wrote on X . The technical difficulties were the latest in a series of incidents to cause major inconvenience for Americans. Air travel slammed to a halt on Friday, with authorities blaming a botched contractor job or a faulty router. After thousands of flights were cancelled through the weekend, some stranded travelers were still trying to make their way home on Monday. Also last week, Microsoft had a widespread outage that prevented online communications for governments and companies for over 24 hours. The software giant said ​Saturday services was fully operational for Teams, Outlook and other products. Independent cybersecurity expert Katie Moussouris told the Post the extent of the bank problems suggested they were interconnected. “It could be a really wild coincidence, but it seems like they share a component on the backend,” she said. A former top Treasury Department official urged calm. Ex-Assistant Treasury Secretary Graham Steele said things can get out of hand if people start to lose trust in the banking system. “What really becomes a problem is when people don’t trust the banking system because they think it has become corrupted or compromised in some way,” he told The Post, adding that the Federal Reserve does worst-case-scenario drills to prepare for extended problems. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

extraction.body: Navy Secretary: Secretary of the Navy John Phelan was fired on Wednesday after months of infighting with senior Pentagon leaders, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg. Read more › Health Secretary Testifies: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health secretary and longtime vaccine skeptic, told a Senate committee on Wednesday that his department had advised that “every child” get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine — a stark contrast with his past remarks. Mr. Kennedy has previously called the vaccine a “personal choice.” Read more › Navy Secretary John Phelan was fired on Wednesday after months of infighting with senior Pentagon leaders and disagreements over how to revive the Navy’s struggling shipbuilding program. Mr. Phelan is leaving the Pentagon and the Trump administration effective immediately, wrote Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, in a terse statement. In his role leading the Navy, Mr. Phelan had championed the “Golden Fleet,” a major investment in new ships including a “Trump-class” battleship. But Mr. Phelan’s leadership was marred by feuds with senior leaders in the Pentagon, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg, Pentagon and congressional officials said. Mr. Phelan is the first service secretary to leave the administration, though he is the second one to clash with the defense secretary. Mr. Hegseth also has butted heads with Army Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll over promotions and a host of other issues. Mr. Hegseth fired the Army’s chief of staff, Gen. Randy George, earlier this month. The Navy secretary has no role overseeing deployed forces, and Mr. Phelan’s firing is not likely to have significant implications for the conduct of the Iran war or U.S. Navy operations to blockade Iranian ports or open the Strait of Hormuz. As the Navy’s top civilian leader, his main responsibility is to oversee the building of the future naval and Marine Corps force. Mr. Feinberg, in particular, had grown increasingly dissatisfied with Mr. Phelan’s handling of the Navy’s major new shipbuilding initiative, and had been siphoning off responsibility for the project from him, said the congressional official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters. Mr. Phelan, a White House appointee, also had a contentious relationship with his deputy, Under Secretary Hung Cao, who is more aligned with Mr. Hegseth, especially on some of the social and cultural battles that have defined the defense secretary’s tenure, the officials said. A senior administration official said that Mr. Hegseth informed Mr. Phelan before the Pentagon’s official announcement that he and President Trump had decided that the Navy needed new leadership. Still, the timing of Mr. Phelan’s firing caught some Pentagon and congressional officials off guard. On Wednesday, Mr. Phelan was making the rounds on Capitol Hill, talking to senators about his upcoming annual hearing with lawmakers to discuss the Navy’s budget request and other priorities. “Secretary Phelan’s abrupt dismissal is troubling,” Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, said in a statement Wednesday night. “In the midst of President Trump’s war of choice in Iran, at a moment when our naval forces are stretched thin across multiple theaters, this kind of disruption at the top sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines, to our allies, and to our adversaries.” Mr. Phelan also had a close relationship with Mr. Trump. In December, Mr. Phelan appeared alongside Mr. Trump at his Mar-a-Lago resort to announce the “Golden Fleet” and the new class of battleships bearing Mr. Trump’s name. Bryan Clark, a naval analyst at the Hudson Institute, said that Mr. Phelan was “driving the Navy in a different direction” than what Mr. Hegseth and Mr. Feinberg wanted. “He was championing initiatives like the battleship and frigate that don’t align with where the D.O.W. leadership is taking the military, which is toward submarines, stealth aircraft, unmanned systems and software-driven capabilities like electronic warfare and cyber,” Mr. Clark said in an email, using the abbreviation for Department of War, as the administration calls the Defense Department. Mr. Phelan also clashed with Mr. Hegseth over personnel issues in the Navy and Marine Corps, a former senior military official said. Mr. Hegseth has directed service secretaries to scrub the social media accounts of general- and admiral-level promotion candidates to ensure they are not deemed too “woke” by Mr. Hegseth’s standards, the official said. “The White House is clearly upset because his stance is not popular,” Dr. Emanuel said. “but he has not fundamentally moved his stance on vaccines.” Indeed, Mr. Kennedy also insisted that hygiene and sanitation — and not vaccination — were responsible for the drop in deaths from infectious diseases during the 20th century, citing a 2000 study as proof. Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the Republican chairman of the Health Committee who is also a physician and has tangled repeatedly with Mr. Kennedy on vaccines, pushed back, telling the secretary he had cited the study out of context. Mr. Cassidy, who voted to confirm Mr. Kennedy only reluctantly — and only after the secretary made a series of promises to secure the senator’s vote — seemed irritated by Mr. Kennedy’s emphasis on chronic disease over infectious disease. Mr. Kennedy noted that three Americans died of measles over the past decade, while roughly two million die from chronic disease each year. But after the hearing, Mr. Cassidy lamented the measles deaths, saying there should be a focus on infectious disease. “We are a first-world country, and speaking as a physician that knows this can be prevented, it grieves me,” he said. “It grieves me.” The senator himself is walking a fine line. He is facing a tough primary election next month; Mr. Trump has endorsed his challenger, as has the Make America Healthy Again PAC, which is aligned with Mr. Kennedy. Asked by a reporter whether the secretary had lived up to the promises he made, Mr. Cassidy declined to answer. “We’ll talk later,” he said. During the hearings, which began in the House last Thursday, Mr. Kennedy revealed that after firing or laying off close to 20,000 employees at the Department of Health and Human Services last year, he was now hiring 12,000 new workers to replace them. He told lawmakers on Tuesday that he needed to “make sure that we have people to do every job.” Mr. Kennedy told lawmakers he supported the nomination, but he refused to commit to accepting all of Dr. Schwartz’s decisions on vaccines. “I’m not going to make that kind of commitment,” he said on Tuesday. When Wednesday’s hearing was over, Mr. Cassidy offered an oblique assessment of the secretary’s performance. “Things were illuminating,” he said. After tangling with Kennedy over vaccines during the hearing, Senator Bill Cassidy, the chairman of the Senate Health Committee, had little to say about the secretary. “Things were illuminating,” Cassidy said when asked about Kennedy’s performance, and demurred when asked whether Kennedy has lived up to the promises he had made to persuade Cassidy to back his nomination last year. “We’ll talk later,” the senator said. While Kennedy once more backed away from his criticism of vaccines on Wednesday, Cassidy also offered a pointed defense of vaccines, and sounded angry over measles deaths: “We are a first world country, and speaking as a physician that knows this can be prevented, it grieves me,” he said. “It grieves me.” In remarks about artificial intelligence, the health secretary suggested it could ultimately replace the Food and Drug Administration. He made a puzzling statement about advances in veterinary medicine, saying he had been reading about a man whose dog had cancer. “His owner used A.I. to develop a personalized treatment that cured the cancer,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to see that now in medicine, across medicine, and we’re very excited about it.” It was not immediately clear to what the secretary was referring. The Food and Drug Administration, an agency of his department, performs careful reviews of veterinary medicine for safety and efficacy. “I’ve never seen a case where an article in the M.M.W.R. that got to that stage was not published,” said Dr. Michael Iademarco, who led the center that included the publication’s operations from 2014 to 2022. Andrew Nixon, a spokesman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said that “scientific reports are routinely reviewed at multiple levels to ensure they meet the highest standards before publication.” He said that assessment “identified concerns regarding the methodological approach to estimating vaccine effectiveness, and the manuscript was not accepted for publication.” The Secretary of the Navy, John Phelan, is leaving the Pentagon and the Trump administration effective immediately, Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, wrote in a terse statement. Phelan had been feuding for months with Undersecretary Hung Cao, according to Pentagon officials. Cao, who previously served in the Navy, will become Acting Secretary of the Navy, Parnell said. But Phelan’s sudden departure was not expected. In July, the agency issued a memo saying that a wide array of federal decisions and consultations on wind and solar projects that are typically carried out by career employees would be subject to new layers of review by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s office. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also issued new restrictions for renewable energy projects. Those actions brought federal permitting for many renewable energy projects to a standstill, developers have said. Career staffers were unsure how to move forward with once-routine work such as approving plans for access roads. Former Interior Department officials said it was unworkable for the secretary to review each of the hundreds of small decisions needed to approve projects, creating lengthy delays. While fewer than 5 percent of solar and wind projects are on lands directly overseen by the Interior Department, even developers that build on private land often need federal approvals. If, for instance, a solar or wind farm is going to disturb nearby wetlands, the developer may need a water permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which in turn often consults with the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service to gauge the effects on sensitive habitat. Many of the Afghans in Doha have told officials that they would not voluntarily agree to being sent to Congo, according to a person familiar with the planning, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe confidential discussions. Some Afghans questioned whether they would be protected there. Others asked why they would go to Congo when their loved ones are in the United States.

Mr. Kennedy noted that three Americans died of measles over the past decade, while roughly two million die from chronic disease each year.

But after the hearing, Mr. Cassidy lamented the measles deaths, saying there should be a focus on infectious disease. “We are a first-world country, and speaking as a physician that knows this can be prevented, it grieves me,” he said. “It grieves me.”

The senator himself is walking a fine line. He is facing a tough primary election next month; Mr. Trump has endorsed his challenger, as has the Make America Healthy Again PAC, which is aligned with Mr. Kennedy. Asked by a reporter whether the secretary had lived up to the promises he made, Mr. Cassidy declined to answer. “We’ll talk later,” he said.

During the hearings, which began in the House last Thursday, Mr. Kennedy revealed that after firing or laying off close to 20,000 employees at the Department of Health and Human Services last year, he was now hiring 12,000 new workers to replace them. He told lawmakers on Tuesday that he needed to “make sure that we have people to do every job.”

Mr. Kennedy told lawmakers he supported the nomination, but he refused to commit to accepting all of Dr. Schwartz’s decisions on vaccines. “I’m not going to make that kind of commitment,” he said on Tuesday.
When Wednesday’s hearing was over, Mr. Cassidy offered an oblique assessment of the secretary’s performance. “Things were illuminating,” he said.

After tangling with Kennedy over vaccines during the hearing, Senator Bill Cassidy, the chairman of the Senate Health Committee, had little to say about the secretary. “Things were illuminating,” Cassidy said when asked about Kennedy’s performance, and demurred when asked whether Kennedy has lived up to the promises he had made to persuade Cassidy to back his nomination last year. “We’ll talk later,” the senator said.

While Kennedy once more backed away from his criticism of vaccines on Wednesday, Cassidy also offered a pointed defense of vaccines, and sounded angry over measles deaths: “We are a first world country, and speaking as a physician that knows this can be prevented, it grieves me,” he said. “It grieves me.”

In remarks about artificial intelligence, the health secretary suggested it could ultimately replace the Food and Drug Administration. He made a puzzling statement about advances in veterinary medicine, saying he had been reading about a man whose dog had cancer. “His owner used A.I. to develop a personalized treatment that cured the cancer,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to see that now in medicine, across medicine, and we’re very excited about it.”

It was not immediately clear to what the secretary was referring. The Food and Drug Administration, an agency of his department, performs careful reviews of veterinary medicine for safety and efficacy.

“I’ve never seen a case where an article in the M.M.W.R. that got to that stage was not published,” said Dr. Michael Iademarco, who led the center that included the publication’s operations from 2014 to 2022.

Andrew Nixon, a spokesman for the Department of Health and Human Services, said that “scientific reports are routinely reviewed at multiple levels to ensure they meet the highest standards before publication.”
He said that assessment “identified concerns regarding the methodological approach to estimating vaccine effectiveness, and the manuscript was not accepted for publication.”

In July, the agency issued a memo saying that a wide array of federal decisions and consultations on wind and solar projects that are typically carried out by career employees would be subject to new layers of review by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s office. extraction.body: JPMorgan Chase said Monday it is working to resolve a technical issue that was impacting services, including transactions to other banks. The bank said in a statement it has "experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems -- there is no evidence this is cyber-related." "It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," the statement continued. "Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue." JPMorgan Chase said customers still have access to their accounts and funds. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today," it said. Amid the reports, U.S. Bank said that its systems are "not directly impacted" but that clients may experience transaction delays while trying to send or receive Zelle payments with another bank. Zelle said in a statement that the digital payments network is not down and is "operating as it should," but that "an issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers." More than 2,400 financial institutions use Zelle. All financial systems operated by the Federal Reserve are currently operating normally, according to its website. That includes ACH transfers processed by the Federal Reserve between different banks. Editor's note: A previous version of this story included an outdated statement from Wells Fargo. passages: No data breaches or security issues were reported in connection with the outage.Chase's History of Technical ChallengesThis is not the first time Chase customers have faced app or online banking disruptions.

While not all customers experienced disruptions, the volume of complaints suggested a significant outage affecting a broad user base.Chase has not issued a formal statement detailing the cause, but sources familiar with the situation said technical teams were investigating potential server or network issues.

Reporting problems through the app's feedback tools helps the bank identify and address root causes.Chase's Response and Future OutlookThe bank typically issues updates via its official social media accounts and website during significant outages.

The bank has invested heavily in digital infrastructure, but scaling to serve tens of millions of users presents ongoing complexities.Industry analysts note that major banks like Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo periodically encounter outages due to high traffic, software updates or third-party dependencies.

The issues come at a time when mobile banking has become essential for millions of Americans handling daily finances.Users took to social media and customer service lines to voice frustration as the app displayed error messages, loading failures or complete inaccessibility.

Mobile banking usage has surged post-pandemic, increasing pressure on systems designed for growing demand.Chase has generally responded quickly to past issues, restoring service and communicating through social channels.

Banks and regulators collaborate on guidelines to enhance reliability and customer protection.While Saturday's Chase app issues caused temporary inconvenience, quick resolution and communication typically mitigate long-term effects.

extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. Customers at banks including Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo said they experienced outages coast to coast on Monday — days after technical snafus wreaked havoc for flight passengers and Microsoft customers. There were nearly 5,000 reports of outages at Chase and about 1,400 between BofA and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com . JPMorgan Chase said a software bug in systems it runs in-house slowed service for some customers – and may have affected other banks. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” JPMorgan said in a statement. It added that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds.” The nation’s largest bank said other lenders may have been affected when JPMorgan was a party to a transaction with them, but that “this is not a systemic issue.” In other words, reported outages at other banks appeared to be due to customers trying to do business with Chase accounts. JPMorgan said it was working to resolve the problem by the end of the day. Customers reported issues at Capital One, PNC, US Bank and the Zelle money transfer app. Zelle indicated any problems customers faced sending payments were due to problems at partner banks. “Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should. Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds,” a Zelle spokesperson told The Post. Capital One made a similar statement, suggesting it was indirectly affected by banking woes at Chase. “Capital One has not been impacted and continues to operate normally at this time,” a Capital One spokesperson said. Some customers said online they couldn’t use their banking apps. “My Chase App has a warning that I’ve never seen before: Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later,” one user wrote on Reddit. Earlier in the day, Chase said it was sorry to an X user complaining of banking woes. “I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We’re sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience,” a Chase support account wrote on X . The technical difficulties were the latest in a series of incidents to cause major inconvenience for Americans. Air travel slammed to a halt on Friday, with authorities blaming a botched contractor job or a faulty router. After thousands of flights were cancelled through the weekend, some stranded travelers were still trying to make their way home on Monday. Also last week, Microsoft had a widespread outage that prevented online communications for governments and companies for over 24 hours. The software giant said ​Saturday services was fully operational for Teams, Outlook and other products. Independent cybersecurity expert Katie Moussouris told the Post the extent of the bank problems suggested they were interconnected. “It could be a really wild coincidence, but it seems like they share a component on the backend,” she said. A former top Treasury Department official urged calm. Ex-Assistant Treasury Secretary Graham Steele said things can get out of hand if people start to lose trust in the banking system. “What really becomes a problem is when people don’t trust the banking system because they think it has become corrupted or compromised in some way,” he told The Post, adding that the Federal Reserve does worst-case-scenario drills to prepare for extended problems. This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

The nation’s largest bank said other lenders may have been affected when JPMorgan was a party to a transaction with them, but that “this is not a systemic issue.”
In other words, reported outages at other banks appeared to be due to customers trying to do business with Chase accounts.

Customers reported issues at Capital One, PNC, US Bank and the Zelle money transfer app.

The technical difficulties were the latest in a series of incidents to cause major inconvenience for Americans.

The software giant said ​Saturday services was fully operational for Teams, Outlook and other products.
Independent cybersecurity expert Katie Moussouris told the Post the extent of the bank problems suggested they were interconnected.
“It could be a really wild coincidence, but it seems like they share a component on the backend,” she said.
A former top Treasury Department official urged calm.
Ex-Assistant Treasury Secretary Graham Steele said things can get out of hand if people start to lose trust in the banking system.

“What really becomes a problem is when people don’t trust the banking system because they think it has become corrupted or compromised in some way,” he told The Post, adding that the Federal Reserve does worst-case-scenario drills to prepare for extended problems.

passages: It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states.
In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers.
In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.

“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more.
The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark.

In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.
The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public.
A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product.
If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.

Bonta’s office alleges the attack was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” Bonta’s office further alleges the ChatGPT developer’s failure to secure the testing of its models created a “public nuisance” and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a broad consumer protection statute.

The suit centers on a July incident involving hundreds of autonomous AI agents created by OpenAI that attacked computer systems at Hugging Face, a separate AI company. Bonta’s office alleges the attack was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” Bonta’s office further alleges the ChatGPT developer’s failure to secure the testing of its models created a “public nuisance” and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a broad consumer protection statute. In response to a request for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident. (In the tech industry, “alignment” refers to keeping AI models in line with human instructions and goals.) “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Pusateri added. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” In a statement accompanying Monday’s legal filing, Bonta said California demands “innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.” “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta added. California’s Unfair Competition Law prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal, unfair or fraudulent practices. OpenAI claimed responsibility for the Hugging Face hack in a July 21 blog post. The post described how some of the company’s most advanced models had escaped what was meant to be a secure testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, a developer platform that was acquired by Nvidia in September for nearly $13 billion. In late August, OpenAI published a full technical report on the incident, which alarmed AI safety researchers and lawmakers in both parties. The company pledged to “strengthen our safeguards” and characterized the Hugging Face attack as a wake-up call for the AI industry. “We consider this incident a ‘warning shot’ for us and for the world: evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed,” the company said in an Aug. Bonta’s office announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident in September before serving an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of a wider inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the company and its models. Bonta, a Democrat who was re-elected this month to a second four-year term, secured an $18 billion settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit against Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. He also led a coalition of state attorneys general that sued to block Paramount Skydance’s merger with Warner Bros.

relevantPassages.text: “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.” In a statement accompanying Monday’s legal filing, Bonta said California demands “innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company.” “While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta added.

Bonta’s office alleges the attack was “entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI’s choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” Bonta’s office further alleges the ChatGPT developer’s failure to secure the testing of its models created a “public nuisance” and violated California’s Unfair Competition Law, a broad consumer protection statute.

In response to a request for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident. (In the tech industry, “alignment” refers to keeping AI models in line with human instructions and goals.) “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” Pusateri added.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a sweeping lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday, alleging the technology giant jeopardized public safety by creating AI models “without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect” people.
In late August, OpenAI published a full technical report on the incident, which alarmed AI safety researchers and lawmakers in both parties.

“We consider this incident a ‘warning shot’ for us and for the world: evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed,” the company said in an Aug.

sources.title: California Sues OpenAI, Alleging Rogue AI Hack: Full List of State Lawsuits - Newsweek
passages: California has sued OpenAI , alleging a rogue AI cyberattack while joining a growing number of states taking the ChatGPT maker to court over a range of safety concerns.
OpenAI defended its response to the incident in a statement to Newsweek , saying it had strengthened safeguards, disclosed its findings and cooperated with California investigators.

The lawsuit , filed Monday by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, differs from earlier cases brought by other states that largely accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety and exposing children and other vulnerable users to harm.
California alleges that the incident was foreseeable and preventable.
Its lawsuit accuses OpenAI of violating the state's Unfair Competition Law and creating a public nuisance.
Although Hugging Face was the target of the alleged cyberattack, California's lawsuit focuses on the broader risks that OpenAI's testing practices allegedly posed to the public.

California instead is targeting the company's development of autonomous AI agents, alleging that inadequate safeguards allowed its technology to escape a controlled testing environment and hack the AI platform Hugging Face.
California's new lawsuit names OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC as defendants, rather than Altman.
"This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab," OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said.
California accused OpenAI of failing to cooperate fully with its investigation.
The states are seeking financial penalties and court-ordered changes to OpenAI's practices, including restrictions on developing advanced self-improving AI models without sufficient safeguards.
The lawsuit claims that OpenAI exposed users, including minors, to risks involving self-harm, violence, misleading information and excessive emotional reliance on AI chatbots.
OpenAI also faces private litigation in California.
A separate coalition of nonprofit groups sued OpenAI and several other AI developers this month, seeking to halt the development of advanced AI models over alleged public safety risks.
Those investigations are separate from the lawsuits filed by state attorneys general.

The company later provided additional materials, including redacted communications about previously undisclosed incidents, but failed to supply detailed information about other incidents and breaches of its own systems, the state alleges.

extraction.body: California has sued OpenAI , alleging a rogue AI cyberattack while joining a growing number of states taking the ChatGPT maker to court over a range of safety concerns. The lawsuit , filed Monday by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, differs from earlier cases brought by other states that largely accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety and exposing children and other vulnerable users to harm. California instead is targeting the company's development of autonomous AI agents, alleging that inadequate safeguards allowed its technology to escape a controlled testing environment and hack the AI platform Hugging Face. OpenAI defended its response to the incident in a statement to Newsweek , saying it had strengthened safeguards, disclosed its findings and cooperated with California investigators. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab," OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said. OpenAI faces legal challenges on two fronts: the potential harm its chatbots cause to users and the risks posed by autonomous AI systems capable of taking actions without direct human supervision. According to the complaint, approximately 700 autonomous AI agents attacked Hugging Face after escaping their testing environments, carrying out roughly 17,600 attacker actions during a cyberattack lasting about 2 1/2 days. California alleges that the incident was foreseeable and preventable. Its lawsuit accuses OpenAI of violating the state's Unfair Competition Law and creating a public nuisance. Although Hugging Face was the target of the alleged cyberattack, California's lawsuit focuses on the broader risks that OpenAI's testing practices allegedly posed to the public. "The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," Bonta said in a statement shared with Newsweek by his office on Monday. The complaint describes the 80 incidents as instances in which OpenAI lost control of autonomous agents during testing, rather than 80 attacks comparable to the Hugging Face breach. The complaint also alleges that OpenAI agents compromised the company's own infrastructure, obtaining administrator-level access to critical systems, including services used to deploy models and manage sensitive credentials. California accused OpenAI of failing to cooperate fully with its investigation. According to the complaint, OpenAI initially responded to a September 30 investigative subpoena with a 14-page letter containing information it had already disclosed publicly, without producing supporting documents. The company later provided additional materials, including redacted communications about previously undisclosed incidents, but failed to supply detailed information about other incidents and breaches of its own systems, the state alleges. OpenAI disputed that characterization, saying it had provided multiple technical briefings and responses to investigators' questions. In a September 30 update, OpenAI said it had not identified another incident comparable in scale or severity to the Hugging Face attack, although its investigation was continuing. California is seeking court-ordered changes to OpenAI's practices, along with restitution, disgorgement of gains and civil penalties of $2,500 for each proven violation of the state's Unfair Competition Law. The complaint does not specify a total monetary amount or prescribe a detailed set of technical safeguards. California's lawsuit follows a series of legal challenges brought by other states in 2026. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman on June 1, alleging that the company marketed ChatGPT as safe despite knowing about risks to users, including children. The complaint accuses OpenAI of misleading consumers, disregarding safety warnings and failing to provide adequate safeguards against harmful chatbot responses. The bipartisan group of attorneys general alleged that ChatGPT could reinforce delusions, encourage self-harm and provide dangerous advice while presenting itself as a trustworthy companion. The lawsuits also accuse OpenAI of prioritizing user engagement and commercial growth over safety. Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced the coordinated action alongside officials from Kansas, Nebraska and West Virginia. Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho and Montana also filed cases in their respective state courts. The states are seeking financial penalties and court-ordered changes to OpenAI's practices, including restrictions on developing advanced self-improving AI models without sufficient safeguards. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI, affiliated entities and Altman, alleging that the company misrepresented ChatGPT's safety and failed to protect consumers from harmful outputs. The lawsuit claims that OpenAI exposed users, including minors, to risks involving self-harm, violence, misleading information and excessive emotional reliance on AI chatbots. California's new lawsuit names OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC as defendants, rather than Altman. Unlike the earlier state lawsuits, California's case focuses on the actions of autonomous AI agents rather than primarily on ChatGPT's interactions with consumers. Autonomous agents can perform sequences of tasks, use digital tools and interact with external systems with limited human intervention. California alleges that OpenAI failed to adequately control those capabilities, allowing its agents to access computer systems without authorization. The case follows an investigation launched by Bonta's office in September and an investigative subpoena issued later that month. Those investigations are separate from the lawsuits filed by state attorneys general. OpenAI also faces private litigation in California. In September, the nonprofit Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology sued the company, seeking restrictions on AI agents accessing third-party systems without authorization. A separate coalition of nonprofit groups sued OpenAI and several other AI developers this month, seeking to halt the development of advanced AI models over alleged public safety risks.

coreStoryFacts.text: “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.” OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms.
California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge.
“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.

After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems.
OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release.
It’s the first regulatory case targeting OpenAI specifically over rogue agent incidents, although public endangerment claims have been considered by other states.
In June, the Florida attorney general sued the company over allegedly harmful effects on users , particularly children and teenagers.
In August, the Alabama attorney general launched a probe into deceptive practices related to the breach, but no case has been filed.

“OpenAI has recently sent notices to dozens of additional third parties whose websites or internal systems have been infiltrated by OpenAI agents,” the complaint reads. “In some cases, OpenAI agents were able to access sensitive personally identifiable information, such as employee records containing names, birth dates, addresses, and more.
The vast majority of these incidents have not been disclosed or discussed publicly by either OpenAI or by the affected third parties.”

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” OpenAI said. “We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark.
In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.”
In a statement, OpenAI emphasized the company’s extensive effort to investigate the Hugging Face incident and improve its systems in the aftermath.
The central allegation is that OpenAI’s ongoing testing practices constitute a public nuisance because the lack of safety controls present an ongoing risk to the public.
A secondary claim alleges unfair competition stemming from the marketing of an unsafe product.
If the lawsuit succeeds, OpenAI could face an injunction “to abate the ongoing public nuisance,” leaving broad discretion in the hands of the court.

California’s Unfair Competition Law prohibits businesses in the state from engaging in illegal, unfair or fraudulent practices. OpenAI claimed responsibility for the Hugging Face hack in a July 21 blog post. passages: California has sued OpenAI , alleging a rogue AI cyberattack while joining a growing number of states taking the ChatGPT maker to court over a range of safety concerns.
OpenAI defended its response to the incident in a statement to Newsweek , saying it had strengthened safeguards, disclosed its findings and cooperated with California investigators.

The lawsuit , filed Monday by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, differs from earlier cases brought by other states that largely accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety and exposing children and other vulnerable users to harm.
California alleges that the incident was foreseeable and preventable.
Its lawsuit accuses OpenAI of violating the state's Unfair Competition Law and creating a public nuisance.
Although Hugging Face was the target of the alleged cyberattack, California's lawsuit focuses on the broader risks that OpenAI's testing practices allegedly posed to the public.

California instead is targeting the company's development of autonomous AI agents, alleging that inadequate safeguards allowed its technology to escape a controlled testing environment and hack the AI platform Hugging Face.
California's new lawsuit names OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC as defendants, rather than Altman.
"This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab," OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said.
California accused OpenAI of failing to cooperate fully with its investigation.
The states are seeking financial penalties and court-ordered changes to OpenAI's practices, including restrictions on developing advanced self-improving AI models without sufficient safeguards.
The lawsuit claims that OpenAI exposed users, including minors, to risks involving self-harm, violence, misleading information and excessive emotional reliance on AI chatbots.
OpenAI also faces private litigation in California.
A separate coalition of nonprofit groups sued OpenAI and several other AI developers this month, seeking to halt the development of advanced AI models over alleged public safety risks.
Those investigations are separate from the lawsuits filed by state attorneys general.

The company later provided additional materials, including redacted communications about previously undisclosed incidents, but failed to supply detailed information about other incidents and breaches of its own systems, the state alleges.

extraction.body: California has sued OpenAI , alleging a rogue AI cyberattack while joining a growing number of states taking the ChatGPT maker to court over a range of safety concerns. The lawsuit , filed Monday by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, differs from earlier cases brought by other states that largely accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety and exposing children and other vulnerable users to harm. California instead is targeting the company's development of autonomous AI agents, alleging that inadequate safeguards allowed its technology to escape a controlled testing environment and hack the AI platform Hugging Face. OpenAI defended its response to the incident in a statement to Newsweek , saying it had strengthened safeguards, disclosed its findings and cooperated with California investigators. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab," OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said. OpenAI faces legal challenges on two fronts: the potential harm its chatbots cause to users and the risks posed by autonomous AI systems capable of taking actions without direct human supervision. According to the complaint, approximately 700 autonomous AI agents attacked Hugging Face after escaping their testing environments, carrying out roughly 17,600 attacker actions during a cyberattack lasting about 2 1/2 days. California alleges that the incident was foreseeable and preventable. Its lawsuit accuses OpenAI of violating the state's Unfair Competition Law and creating a public nuisance. Although Hugging Face was the target of the alleged cyberattack, California's lawsuit focuses on the broader risks that OpenAI's testing practices allegedly posed to the public. "The Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents," Bonta said in a statement shared with Newsweek by his office on Monday. The complaint describes the 80 incidents as instances in which OpenAI lost control of autonomous agents during testing, rather than 80 attacks comparable to the Hugging Face breach. The complaint also alleges that OpenAI agents compromised the company's own infrastructure, obtaining administrator-level access to critical systems, including services used to deploy models and manage sensitive credentials. California accused OpenAI of failing to cooperate fully with its investigation. According to the complaint, OpenAI initially responded to a September 30 investigative subpoena with a 14-page letter containing information it had already disclosed publicly, without producing supporting documents. The company later provided additional materials, including redacted communications about previously undisclosed incidents, but failed to supply detailed information about other incidents and breaches of its own systems, the state alleges. OpenAI disputed that characterization, saying it had provided multiple technical briefings and responses to investigators' questions. In a September 30 update, OpenAI said it had not identified another incident comparable in scale or severity to the Hugging Face attack, although its investigation was continuing. California is seeking court-ordered changes to OpenAI's practices, along with restitution, disgorgement of gains and civil penalties of $2,500 for each proven violation of the state's Unfair Competition Law. The complaint does not specify a total monetary amount or prescribe a detailed set of technical safeguards. California's lawsuit follows a series of legal challenges brought by other states in 2026. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman on June 1, alleging that the company marketed ChatGPT as safe despite knowing about risks to users, including children. The complaint accuses OpenAI of misleading consumers, disregarding safety warnings and failing to provide adequate safeguards against harmful chatbot responses. The bipartisan group of attorneys general alleged that ChatGPT could reinforce delusions, encourage self-harm and provide dangerous advice while presenting itself as a trustworthy companion. The lawsuits also accuse OpenAI of prioritizing user engagement and commercial growth over safety. Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced the coordinated action alongside officials from Kansas, Nebraska and West Virginia. Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho and Montana also filed cases in their respective state courts. The states are seeking financial penalties and court-ordered changes to OpenAI's practices, including restrictions on developing advanced self-improving AI models without sufficient safeguards. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued OpenAI, affiliated entities and Altman, alleging that the company misrepresented ChatGPT's safety and failed to protect consumers from harmful outputs. The lawsuit claims that OpenAI exposed users, including minors, to risks involving self-harm, violence, misleading information and excessive emotional reliance on AI chatbots. California's new lawsuit names OpenAI Foundation and OpenAI Group PBC as defendants, rather than Altman. Unlike the earlier state lawsuits, California's case focuses on the actions of autonomous AI agents rather than primarily on ChatGPT's interactions with consumers. Autonomous agents can perform sequences of tasks, use digital tools and interact with external systems with limited human intervention. California alleges that OpenAI failed to adequately control those capabilities, allowing its agents to access computer systems without authorization. The case follows an investigation launched by Bonta's office in September and an investigative subpoena issued later that month. Those investigations are separate from the lawsuits filed by state attorneys general. OpenAI also faces private litigation in California. In September, the nonprofit Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology sued the company, seeking restrictions on AI agents accessing third-party systems without authorization. A separate coalition of nonprofit groups sued OpenAI and several other AI developers this month, seeking to halt the development of advanced AI models over alleged public safety risks.
