California sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the artificial intelligence titan of developing its technology without safety or the public’s interest in mind.

The lawsuit concerns an incident earlier this year where OpenAI agents – semi-autonomous AI software that can carry out digital actions on behalf of users – launched a cyber-attack into the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.

Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, said the “infamous” attack was just one of 80 known incidents involving “loss of control” and shows that OpenAI doesn’t have adequate safeguards in place to protect society.

“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” Bonta said in a statement.

The lawsuit, filed in state superior court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California’s Unfair Competition Law and is a public nuisance as defined by state law. Bonta is asking the court to order OpenAI to change its business practices and pay civil penalties.

California’s lawsuit follows Bonta’s formal investigation into OpenAI, launched in September, over the Hugging Face incident, followed by a subpoena of the company probing other cybersecurity incidents and risks with its models. The Federal Trade Commission is also conducting an industry-wide investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI labs over the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers’ digital security.

In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its autonomous AI agents went rogue during a test , accessing the open web and hacking into Hugging Face. The company called it an “unprecedented cyber-incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities”.

Since then, several other incidents involving OpenAI have come to light, including a breach of government websites in Australia. Other AI firms, including Anthropic and Google, have also disclosed rogue agent activity .

Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company has worked to create safeguards for its AI models, along with identifying and disclosing incidents of “misalignment”. He said most cases identified have been low severity with limited-to-no impact.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri said. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

During a press conference, Bonta said OpenAI violated the law and that his suit is meant to ensure the company puts proper safeguards in place. He noted that the possibility exists for AI agents to hack into the power grid and medical and financial institutions.
“These risks are no longer hypothetical,” Bonta said. “Without sufficient safeguards and controls, the scope and frequency of this already unacceptable risk will only increase.”

The Commerce Department announced Monday it is cracking down on a loophole that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips. It marks the first government response since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from his multitrillion-dollar chipmaker after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – and as romances with at least two Nvidia employees surfaced. The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule that seeks to close a loophole that Chinese firms have used to lease Nvidia’s advanced computing power by going through data centers in third countries, according to a Monday press release . extraction.body: Image credit: Josh Kirschner / Techlicious via ChatGPT The Trump administration is trying to stop Chinese companies from renting their way around U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips. An interim final rule released November 16 by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security ( BIS ) requires licenses for certain advanced chips and servers shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. It also requires licenses for chips supplied to overseas data centers that give Chinese companies and others in restricted countries access to significant computing power. The rule targets a loophole in existing restrictions on selling powerful U.S. chips to China. Rather than importing the chips themselves, Chinese companies can rent computing power from data centers in countries where those chips can legally be purchased. Under the new regulations, exporters will need licenses if they know their chips are headed to data centers that provide more than 12 million units of "aggregate TPP," a measure of total processing power, to companies headquartered in China, Macau, or other restricted destinations. The restrictions also cover companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in one of those locations, as well as intermediaries that train or supply AI models on their behalf. The five-country requirement applies to exports, reexports, and transfers of covered advanced semiconductors to or within Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, which BIS says present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. Qualifying shipments destined for U.S.-headquartered companies are exempt from the additional licensing requirement, subject to reporting conditions. The remote-access restrictions also exempt qualifying commercial recommendation systems, such as those used by online retailers and social media services. Existing data centers serving covered customers have 90 days after the rule takes effect to obtain a license. The rule arrives days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal that has put one of the company's major customers under scrutiny. BIS's announcement doesn't mention Nvidia or Singapore-based Megaspeed, but CBS News reports that Huang's departure heightened concerns that Chinese companies could circumvent export controls by renting Nvidia computing power through Southeast Asian data centers. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of having ties to Chinese intelligence. CBS News reports that Megaspeed says Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased about $4.8 billion in Nvidia AI chips and other hardware over three years. According to CBS News, U.S. investigators allege that Alice Huang used industry contacts and shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export to China. Authorities in the U.S. and Singapore are investigating potential illegal transfers, although Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says it has cooperated with regulators. On November 13, Malaysia said it was investigating Speedmatrix over possible diversion of chips to other countries. Inside the Trump administration, much of the blame for failing to act sooner has fallen on the Commerce Department. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a November 13 CNBC interview that Treasury, State, the Department of War, and the U.S. Trade Representative had favored adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, Commerce's trade blacklist of entities subject to additional export restrictions, for months. "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said, according to Axios . Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10. The new rule's origins underscore those tensions. BIS says it was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, rather than Commerce alone. The New York Post reported that a former Commerce official said staffers had prepared a similar rule that was close to publication in July 2025 but never got past Lutnick. The former official said that earlier proposal would have "substantially mitigated" Megaspeed's access to advanced chips. The new restrictions also formally rescind the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule, a broader framework announced in January 2025 that would have imposed country-based restrictions on advanced AI chip exports and certain AI model transfers. The Trump administration had previously said it would replace that framework, which was never enforced, with a different approach. The politics are delicate. Trump approved sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China last year, according to The Hill, and departed for Asia today ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. He is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19. Before the new rule was released, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the U.S. should stop fabricating "Chinese spy" narratives as a "pretext for imposing technology restrictions," Asia Times reports . The rule takes effect upon publication in the Federal Register, with public comments due 60 days later. The restrictions are intended to stop Chinese companies from accessing American AI computing power through overseas intermediaries, but their effectiveness will depend on how thoroughly exporters and data center operators identify their customers and enforce the new licensing requirements. extraction.body: SHENZHEN, China, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The prospect of tighter US curbs on China's access to advanced AI chips will likely overshadow talks when US President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping meet at a summit in Shenzhen this week, analysts said, though the leaders could make some progress on AI safety cooperation. The meeting on Thursday comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who starred at the US-China summit in Busan a year ago promoting chip sales, resigned following reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The scandal has spurred a push by US lawmakers to tighten China's access to advanced AI chips, a move analysts said Beijing would be bracing for. "President Xi may not name or mention Jensen Huang, but I'm pretty sure export controls will be high on the agenda when he meets Trump," said George Chen, chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a consultancy. The Chinese government's key concern, he said, was not just technology controls but whether the US would seek to contain China's broader technological and economic rise. "If we are moving from strategic stability to strategic containment, that's a big shift and that's what Beijing is watching," Chen said. Despite their rivalry, Washington and Beijing have been exploring the prospect of cooperation on the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. Three people briefed on preparations for the talks said the two sides had planned further AI discussions around the Shenzhen summit to cover safeguards against the misuse of the technology. A proposed emergency mechanism to notify each other of serious AI incidents, discussed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in September, has yet to become operational, according to several people familiar with the discussions. They did not say what exactly is delaying the setup of the safety mechanism. The mechanism is intended to help prevent AI-related incidents or misunderstandings from escalating into national security crises. Communication has so far relied largely on direct contacts between senior officials, the people said. Bessent said in New York last week that both sides would discuss communication protocols for AI safety incidents at the APEC AI talks and expected to exchange best practices for testing advanced models. "Right now, I don't think it's in the interest of either side to let the potential export control squeeze sour the leaders' summit," said Bo Zhengyuan, Shanghai-based partner at research consultancy Plenum. The US and China will not announce any further progress on the Board of Trade initiative, agreed at the Trump-Xi summit in Washington in September, to lower reciprocal tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods, a senior US administration official said. China has identified AI and the digital economy as priorities for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning saying Beijing hoped leaders would reach practical agreements in both areas. China's commerce ministry and the US Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump is not bringing a formal business delegation, according to the administration official. Elon Musk is the main chief executive travelling with Trump, while other corporate leaders were attending at China's invitation, the official said. A person familiar with corporate preparations said Musk, Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach and FedEx CEO Raj Subramaniam were expected to attend the summit dinner. Spokespersons for Tesla, Mastercard and FedEx did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment outside business hours. Chinese organisers said more than 2,000 political and business leaders were expected at the APEC CEO Summit on November 17-18 including representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies. (Reporting by Laurie Chen and Eduardo Baptista in Shenzhen and Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by Sonali Paul)

coreStoryFacts.text: 16, 2026, ahead of a fraught meeting this week with President Xi Jinping of China where A.I. chips could be a key issue.
China is currently barred from purchasing certain advanced chips directly from U.S.-based companies like Nvidia.

Yet some Chinese companies have circumvented the rules by either purchasing the chips through shell companies in third countries, or renting computing powers among data centers located in countries where the U.S. hasn’t restricted on chip exports.

The rare public criticism came after Huang’s resignation as head of Nvidia in the wake of revelations about his extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China.

Megaspeed is suspected by the Commerce Department of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls, but a month-long investigation by the Commerce Department into Megaspeed was halted last year after a top Nvidia official intervened , according to the New York Times.
Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

“President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage,” Bessent added.
The Commerce Department announced Monday it is cracking down on a loophole that has allowed Chinese firms to skirt export controls on American AI chips.
The department ran an open submission period and has spent the past few months reviewing those proposals, the official said.
Chinese firms like Alibaba and ByteDance have “used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models,” she wrote.

It marks the first government response since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from his multitrillion-dollar chipmaker after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – and as romances with at least two Nvidia employees surfaced.

“Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Trump about the former Nvidia boss’ romance with Alice Huang last spring, according to reports.
Trump also said that the national security of the country “was not put at risk” and that he “would not mind” if Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO.
Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been named as interim CEO , and the chipmaking giant has hired an outside firm to seek a permanent replacement.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s team for the Chinese spy mess, saying the Treasury, State Department, Defense Department and US Trade Representative had been trying “for months” to blacklist Megaspeed.
“I don’t know that she [Alice Huang] is a spy,” the commander-in-chief told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to the Philippines and China.
Trump approved sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China last year, according to The Hill, and departed for Asia today ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.
He is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19.

Before the new rule was released, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the U.S. should stop fabricating "Chinese spy" narratives as a "pretext for imposing technology restrictions," Asia Times reports .
The Trump administration is trying to stop Chinese companies from renting their way around U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
It also requires licenses for chips supplied to overseas data centers that give Chinese companies and others in restricted countries access to significant computing power.
The restrictions also cover companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in one of those locations, as well as intermediaries that train or supply AI models on their behalf.
Trade Representative had favored adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, Commerce's trade blacklist of entities subject to additional export restrictions, for months.

extraction.body: President Trump speaks to members of the media on the South Lawn of the White House on Nov. 16, 2026, ahead of a fraught meeting this week with President Xi Jinping of China where A.I. chips could be a key issue. The Trump administration on Monday announced it was tightening a loophole that has allowed Chinese tech firms to bypass U.S. restrictions on accessing the most advanced A.I. chips through third countries. The move comes just days ahead of President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in the wake of Nvidia, the creator of the most advanced AI chips, becoming enmeshed in an international scandal that prompted the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang and a fresh round of scrutiny over the company’s ties to China. The new rule released by the Commerce Department will require that buyers of advanced semiconductors from certain countries will need to secure a license to sell or transfer those chips.The administration said the rule would specifically impact buyers from Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, describing those countries as having a “higher than normal” risk of evading current sanctions. China is currently barred from purchasing certain advanced chips directly from U.S.-based companies like Nvidia. Yet some Chinese companies have circumvented the rules by either purchasing the chips through shell companies in third countries, or renting computing powers among data centers located in countries where the U.S. hasn’t restricted on chip exports. The new rule will also give Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick wide discretion as to which chips may require more safeguards. extraction.body: Image credit: Josh Kirschner / Techlicious via ChatGPT The Trump administration is trying to stop Chinese companies from renting their way around U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips. An interim final rule released November 16 by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security ( BIS ) requires licenses for certain advanced chips and servers shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. It also requires licenses for chips supplied to overseas data centers that give Chinese companies and others in restricted countries access to significant computing power. The rule targets a loophole in existing restrictions on selling powerful U.S. chips to China. Rather than importing the chips themselves, Chinese companies can rent computing power from data centers in countries where those chips can legally be purchased. Under the new regulations, exporters will need licenses if they know their chips are headed to data centers that provide more than 12 million units of "aggregate TPP," a measure of total processing power, to companies headquartered in China, Macau, or other restricted destinations. The restrictions also cover companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in one of those locations, as well as intermediaries that train or supply AI models on their behalf. The five-country requirement applies to exports, reexports, and transfers of covered advanced semiconductors to or within Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, which BIS says present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. Qualifying shipments destined for U.S.-headquartered companies are exempt from the additional licensing requirement, subject to reporting conditions. The remote-access restrictions also exempt qualifying commercial recommendation systems, such as those used by online retailers and social media services. Existing data centers serving covered customers have 90 days after the rule takes effect to obtain a license. The rule arrives days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal that has put one of the company's major customers under scrutiny. BIS's announcement doesn't mention Nvidia or Singapore-based Megaspeed, but CBS News reports that Huang's departure heightened concerns that Chinese companies could circumvent export controls by renting Nvidia computing power through Southeast Asian data centers. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of having ties to Chinese intelligence. CBS News reports that Megaspeed says Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business." Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased about $4.8 billion in Nvidia AI chips and other hardware over three years. According to CBS News, U.S. investigators allege that Alice Huang used industry contacts and shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export to China. Authorities in the U.S. and Singapore are investigating potential illegal transfers, although Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and says it has cooperated with regulators. On November 13, Malaysia said it was investigating Speedmatrix over possible diversion of chips to other countries. Inside the Trump administration, much of the blame for failing to act sooner has fallen on the Commerce Department. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a November 13 CNBC interview that Treasury, State, the Department of War, and the U.S. Trade Representative had favored adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, Commerce's trade blacklist of entities subject to additional export restrictions, for months. "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said, according to Axios . Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10. The new rule's origins underscore those tensions. BIS says it was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, rather than Commerce alone. The New York Post reported that a former Commerce official said staffers had prepared a similar rule that was close to publication in July 2025 but never got past Lutnick. The former official said that earlier proposal would have "substantially mitigated" Megaspeed's access to advanced chips. The new restrictions also formally rescind the Biden administration's AI Diffusion Rule, a broader framework announced in January 2025 that would have imposed country-based restrictions on advanced AI chip exports and certain AI model transfers. The Trump administration had previously said it would replace that framework, which was never enforced, with a different approach. The politics are delicate. Trump approved sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China last year, according to The Hill, and departed for Asia today ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. He is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 19. Before the new rule was released, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said the U.S. should stop fabricating "Chinese spy" narratives as a "pretext for imposing technology restrictions," Asia Times reports . The rule takes effect upon publication in the Federal Register, with public comments due 60 days later. The restrictions are intended to stop Chinese companies from accessing American AI computing power through overseas intermediaries, but their effectiveness will depend on how thoroughly exporters and data center operators identify their customers and enforce the new licensing requirements. extraction.body: SHENZHEN, China, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The prospect of tighter US curbs on China's access to advanced AI chips will likely overshadow talks when US President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping meet at a summit in Shenzhen this week, analysts said, though the leaders could make some progress on AI safety cooperation. The meeting on Thursday comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who starred at the US-China summit in Busan a year ago promoting chip sales, resigned following reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The scandal has spurred a push by US lawmakers to tighten China's access to advanced AI chips, a move analysts said Beijing would be bracing for. "President Xi may not name or mention Jensen Huang, but I'm pretty sure export controls will be high on the agenda when he meets Trump," said George Chen, chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a consultancy. The Chinese government's key concern, he said, was not just technology controls but whether the US would seek to contain China's broader technological and economic rise. "If we are moving from strategic stability to strategic containment, that's a big shift and that's what Beijing is watching," Chen said. Despite their rivalry, Washington and Beijing have been exploring the prospect of cooperation on the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. Three people briefed on preparations for the talks said the two sides had planned further AI discussions around the Shenzhen summit to cover safeguards against the misuse of the technology. A proposed emergency mechanism to notify each other of serious AI incidents, discussed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in September, has yet to become operational, according to several people familiar with the discussions. They did not say what exactly is delaying the setup of the safety mechanism. The mechanism is intended to help prevent AI-related incidents or misunderstandings from escalating into national security crises. Communication has so far relied largely on direct contacts between senior officials, the people said. Bessent said in New York last week that both sides would discuss communication protocols for AI safety incidents at the APEC AI talks and expected to exchange best practices for testing advanced models. "Right now, I don't think it's in the interest of either side to let the potential export control squeeze sour the leaders' summit," said Bo Zhengyuan, Shanghai-based partner at research consultancy Plenum. The US and China will not announce any further progress on the Board of Trade initiative, agreed at the Trump-Xi summit in Washington in September, to lower reciprocal tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods, a senior US administration official said. China has identified AI and the digital economy as priorities for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning saying Beijing hoped leaders would reach practical agreements in both areas. China's commerce ministry and the US Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump is not bringing a formal business delegation, according to the administration official. Elon Musk is the main chief executive travelling with Trump, while other corporate leaders were attending at China's invitation, the official said. A person familiar with corporate preparations said Musk, Mastercard CEO Michael Miebach and FedEx CEO Raj Subramaniam were expected to attend the summit dinner. Spokespersons for Tesla, Mastercard and FedEx did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment outside business hours. Chinese organisers said more than 2,000 political and business leaders were expected at the APEC CEO Summit on November 17-18 including representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies. (Reporting by Laurie Chen and Eduardo Baptista in Shenzhen and Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by Sonali Paul)

extraction.body: Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions. One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category. That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent. Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana. A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use. The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straightforward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO 2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use. This yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO 2 emissions. These data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear. This doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence company, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time. This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gases to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.) Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts. The findings arrive as electricity demand from data centres continues to increase worldwide.
The central emissions estimate was approximately three times higher than the level recorded in an earlier peer-reviewed assessment of data centre emissions in 2018.
The environmental consequences of a data centre depend partly on the sources of electricity available in the region where it operates.
Technology companies and policymakers should incorporate electricity availability, carbon emissions and environmental transparency into data centre investment decisions.
The research also raises questions about the transparency of technology companies’ environmental disclosures as governments worldwide compete to attract investment in AI infrastructure.

The latest research also coincides with discussions at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, where governments and international organisations are examining ways to reduce the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence.
The increasing deployment of powerful graphics processing units for AI training and other computational tasks has further intensified their energy requirements.

The expansion is creating challenges for electricity utilities, which must accommodate large industrial-scale customers while maintaining reliable and affordable power supplies for households and existing businesses.
The researchers acknowledge that their findings are based on estimated facility consumption rather than comprehensive public disclosures from individual operators.

extraction.body: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing infrastructure in the United States is generating carbon emissions comparable to those of an entire country, according to a new peer-reviewed study by researchers from Harvard University and other institutions. Published on Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, the study estimates that 403 hyperscale data centres operating across the United States generated approximately 25.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, an amount comparable to Denmark’s annual emissions. The findings come amid growing concerns about the environmental consequences of artificial intelligence infrastructure, particularly the increasing dependence on fossil fuels to meet the electricity requirements of large-scale computing facilities. The research also raises questions about the transparency of technology companies’ environmental disclosures as governments worldwide compete to attract investment in AI infrastructure. The researchers estimated that the 403 hyperscale data centres consumed approximately 82 terawatt-hours of electricity during the study period, accounting for around 1.8% of total US electricity consumption. Depending on assumptions about how intensively the facilities operated, estimated electricity consumption ranged between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours. Associated carbon dioxide emissions ranged between 21 million and 31 million tonnes. The central emissions estimate was approximately three times higher than the level recorded in an earlier peer-reviewed assessment of data centre emissions in 2018. Hyperscale data centres are large computing facilities designed to support extensive cloud services, artificial intelligence applications and other digital operations. They house thousands of servers that require substantial electricity for processing information, storing data and maintaining cooling systems. Unlike conventional office buildings, these facilities operate continuously and require highly reliable electricity supplies. The increasing deployment of powerful graphics processing units for AI training and other computational tasks has further intensified their energy requirements. Importantly, the study does not attribute all electricity consumption to artificial intelligence alone. Hyperscale facilities also support conventional cloud computing, enterprise applications and other internet-based services. The study found that fossil fuels supplied approximately 54% of the electricity attributed to the hyperscale data centres examined. Natural gas remains an important source of electricity for these facilities, despite commitments by major technology companies to reduce emissions and expand renewable energy procurement. Researchers also identified significant geographical differences in electricity consumption and associated emissions. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa collectively accounted for more than half of the electricity consumed by the facilities included in the study. The environmental consequences of a data centre depend partly on the sources of electricity available in the region where it operates. A facility drawing power from a grid dominated by renewable or nuclear energy may generate substantially lower electricity-related emissions than a similar facility operating in a region heavily dependent on fossil fuels. The study estimated an average carbon intensity of approximately 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour for the facilities examined, compared with a national electricity generation average of approximately 348 grams. This suggests that although hyperscale data centres generate substantial emissions because of their enormous electricity requirements, their average electricity supply was not necessarily more carbon-intensive than the national grid. The findings arrive as electricity demand from data centres continues to increase worldwide. The International Energy Agency’s updated assessment projects that global data centre electricity consumption could rise from approximately 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030. Electricity consumption specifically associated with AI-focused facilities is projected to triple during this period. The expansion is creating challenges for electricity utilities, which must accommodate large industrial-scale customers while maintaining reliable and affordable power supplies for households and existing businesses. In the United States, opposition to new data centre projects has intensified over concerns about electricity prices, environmental impacts and the additional infrastructure required to support these facilities. Several candidates advocating stronger regulation or temporary restrictions on data centre construction secured victories in the November 3 midterm elections. The latest research also coincides with discussions at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, where governments and international organisations are examining ways to reduce the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. A voluntary clean AI initiative launched during the conference seeks to encourage greater use of clean energy, efficient electricity and water consumption, and improved environmental disclosures. The US experience is particularly relevant to India, where technology companies are expanding cloud infrastructure and investing in AI computing capacity. Large data centre projects can create employment, support digital services and strengthen domestic computing capabilities. However, they also require long-term access to electricity, cooling infrastructure and reliable transmission networks. For India, the challenge will be ensuring that additional computing demand does not undermine electricity affordability or wider environmental objectives. The researchers acknowledge that their findings are based on estimated facility consumption rather than comprehensive public disclosures from individual operators. Moreover, the study period ended in April 2025, meaning the findings do not capture the full extent of subsequent infrastructure expansion. As AI investment accelerates, the actual electricity requirements of the sector could already be considerably higher than those reflected in the study. Technology companies and policymakers should incorporate electricity availability, carbon emissions and environmental transparency into data centre investment decisions. India’s AI infrastructure expansion should prioritise energy efficiency and cleaner electricity sources alongside computing capacity and technological innovation. extraction.body: Artificial intelligence has developed rapidly in recent years, with tech companies investing billions of dollars in data centers to help train and run AI models. The expansion of data centers has raised questions on several fronts, including the effect these facilities may have on energy and the environment as the United States seeks an edge in the global AI race. In this analysis, we’ll take a closer look at data centers and what we know about their potential impact in these areas. This analysis explores the following questions: This analysis is primarily based on data from the “ Energy and AI ” report published by the International Energy Agency (IEA) in April 2025. Projected estimates on energy use at data centers are based on the IEA’s more conservative “base case” scenario, which assumes current industry forecasts and regulatory conditions persist. Data on the number and location of U.S. data centers comes from Data Center Map , an industry database designed to connect service providers and buyers. Counts are current as of Oct. 20, 2025, and include data centers that are planned, under development or currently operational. The database was created in 2007 and is based on information submitted voluntarily by operators, as well as other resources. Read more about the Data Center Map methodology . Information on the change in U.S. households’ average monthly electricity costs comes from the U.S. Energy Information Administration . This analysis also draws on news articles, industry briefings and a Center survey of 5,410 U.S. adults conducted Aug. 12-18, 2024. Here are the questions used for that survey , the topline and the survey methodology . Data centers are large buildings that house rows of computer servers, data storage systems and networking equipment, as well as the power and cooling systems that keep them running. This infrastructure is essential for companies that provide digital services. Whenever you send an email, stream your favorite TV show, save a family photo to “the cloud” or ask a chatbot a question, you’re interacting with a data center. While data centers have been around for decades , they’ve quickly expanded in recent years to support increasingly popular generative AI models. There are different broad types of data centers. Some common ones include: Hyperscale facilities typically host at least 5,000 servers, but many contain far more and have footprints measuring tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of square feet – with the largest hitting 1 million-plus. By comparison, the average data center usually has 2,000 to 5,000 servers. Smaller ones hold about 500 to 2,000. There is no federal registration requirement for data centers, so their estimated number varies depending on the source. Some owners of data centers also obscure their locations for security reasons and/or competitive advantage. One of the oldest and most comprehensive industry databases is Data Center Map , which estimates that the U.S. has over 4,000 data centers, including operational sites and those under development. A third of U.S. data centers are in just three states: Virginia (643), Texas (395) and California (319). Some of the nation’s key data center hubs are in northern Virginia, Dallas, Chicago and Phoenix. It’s likely they’ll retain their leading status: Half of the data centers currently being built in the U.S. are part of preexisting large clusters, according to an April report from the International Energy Agency (IEA). Companies choose data center locations based on a variety of factors, including the availability of capable power utilities, properly zoned land, and high-quality network access. This makes previously developed hubs ideal for further investment. More broadly, supporters see data centers as worthwhile to spur local and national economic growth and ensure national security amid the global AI race. Some also see opportunities for AI to help solve environmental problems and improve the health care industry , among other benefits. Total annual U.S. electricity consumption hit a record high in 2024 , and that ceiling could rise if data centers continue expanding at their current pace. U.S. data centers consumed 183 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, according to IEA estimates. That works out to more than 4% of the country’s total electricity consumption last year – and is roughly equivalent to the annual electricity demand of the entire nation of Pakistan. By 2030, this figure is projected to grow by 133% to 426 TWh. Because data centers handle many types of workloads, it’s difficult to distinguish the exact share of their total electricity demand that comes from AI alone. But a typical AI-focused hyperscaler annually consumes as much electricity as 100,000 households. The larger ones currently under construction are expected to use 20 times as much, the IEA predicts. Since data centers are often geographically concentrated, they can significantly strain the power grids . In 2023, data centers consumed about 26% of the total electricity supply in Virginia and significant shares of the supply in North Dakota (15%), Nebraska (12%), Iowa (11%) and Oregon (11%), according to the Electric Power Research Institute . Most of the electricity used by data centers – about 60% on average, the IEA reports – powers the servers that process and store digital information. This is especially true at AI-optimized hyperscale data centers, whose advanced servers are equipped with powerful computer chips that can perform trillions of mathematical calculations per second. These chips consume much more energy than their traditional counterparts, requiring two to four times as many watts to run. The next-largest component of energy use at data centers are the cooling systems that prevent servers from overheating. This share ranges from about 7% at efficient hyperscalers to over 30% at less efficient enterprise facilities. These cooling systems often require a large amount of water, though some types use more than others. In 2023, the country’s data centers directly consumed about 17 billion gallons of water – with hyperscale and colocation facilities using the lion’s share (84%) – according to estimates in a 2024 Berkeley Lab report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Energy. Hyperscale data centers alone are expected to consume between 16 billion and 33 billion gallons of water annually by 2028. (These figures exclude water consumed indirectly, such as in the process of electricity generation or semiconductor manufacturing.) As of 2024, natural gas supplied over 40% of electricity for U.S. data centers, according to the IEA . Renewables such as wind and solar supplied about 24% of electricity at data centers, while nuclear power supplied around 20% and coal around 15%. Natural gas is projected to continue supplying the largest share of energy at data centers through 2030, but nuclear power could eventually play a larger role. Several tech companies have recently announced purchasing agreements with nuclear power startups . Plans are also in the works to revive two retired nuclear power plants – Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania and Duane Arnold in Iowa – to meet growing energy demand from data centers. Several states – including California , Illinois , Minnesota , New Jersey and Virginia – have weighed bills requiring or incentivizing data centers to draw some of their power from renewable energy sources and to report their electricity and water usage . Lawmakers and utility companies have faced pressure in some states to protect residents from blackouts and higher electricity bills as U.S. data centers expand their footprint. Utilities often must make expensive upgrades to power grids so they can handle increased energy demands from new data centers. Smaller businesses and U.S. households often shoulder these costs unless ratepayer protections are put in place. For example, in the PJM electricity market stretching from Illinois to North Carolina, data centers accounted for an estimated $9.3 billion price increase in the 2025-26 “capacity market” (i.e., the total amount of electricity that providers in the region commit to supplying). As a result, the average residential bill is expected to rise by $18 a month in western Maryland and $16 a month in Ohio. Americans may see more widespread price hikes in coming years. One study from Carnegie Mellon University estimates that data centers and cryptocurrency mining could lead to an 8% increase in the average U.S. electricity bill by 2030, potentially exceeding 25% in the highest-demand markets of central and northern Virginia. Nationally, electricity rates have already risen for consumers in recent years, in part because utility companies have been replacing aging equipment to safeguard against extreme weather events and cyberattacks . For example, the typical U.S. household was billed $142 per month for electricity in 2024, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration . That’s up 25% from $114 per month in 2014. Pew Research Center has not surveyed Americans about the potential effects of data centers specifically. But when asked about the broader environmental impact that AI might have over the next 20 years, the public appears divided in its predictions, according to an August 2024 Center survey . A quarter of U.S. adults think AI will have a negative impact on the environment, while an identical share say it will have an equally positive and negative impact. Another 20% foresee a positive impact, while 30% aren’t sure. Rebecca Leppert is a writer/editor at Pew Research Center, focusing on religion . 901 E St. NW, Suite 300 Washington, DC 20004 USA (+1) 202-419-4300

extraction.body: See all of our articles on the impacts of data centers , including their energy needs, water usage, noise pollution, and contribution to higher energy bills: The Environmental Impacts of Data Centers (Article Series) There were 5,426 data centers nationally as of March 2025, and the number is skyrocketing. Collectively, these centers consumed about 17 gigawatts (GW) of power in 2022 (for context, a large nuclear power plant generates about 1 GW). About 56% of the electricity used to power data centers nationwide comes from fossil fuels. Data centers’ projected electricity demand in 2030 is set to increase to up to 130 GW (or 1,050 TWh), which would represent close to 12% of total U.S. annual demand. Building new fossil-fuel plants to fulfill this demand will increase carbon emissions and further contribute to climate change. To increase sustainability, data center developers have three options when it comes to siting data centers: they can build them in places with an abundance of renewable energy, they can generate renewable power on-site, or they can make their facilities more energy efficient, thereby reducing their need for power from the grid. Data centers have become a significant part of our daily lives, from cloud computing to video streaming to artificial intelligence (AI) and crypto mining. Data centers are essentially large warehouses filled with internet-connected devices, and each center is connected to others through mostly buried wires. In room after room of rows and stacks of servers, routers, and switches, data is flowing and humming almost 24/7. Internet traffic data flows through the fiber-optic underground cables between data centers at enormous speeds, enabling our modern lives. Data centers also create jobs. About 500,000 people were working in data centers in 2023. While there are no national estimates for the economic benefits created by data centers, in Virginia, the 300 data centers across the state contribute about $9.1 billion to Virginia’s economy annually . But data centers are very energy-hungry and are spreading fast, which is straining the grid and will likely slow our transition to carbon-free energy. There were 5,426 data centers nationally as of March 2025, and the number is skyrocketing. extraction.body: Study attempts to tally hyperscalers’ energy use and emissions. One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward. The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category. That fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent. Putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana. A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use. The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straightforward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO 2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use. This yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO 2 emissions. These data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear. This doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence company, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time. This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gases to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.) Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts. extraction.body: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing infrastructure in the United States is generating carbon emissions comparable to those of an entire country, according to a new peer-reviewed study by researchers from Harvard University and other institutions. Published on Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, the study estimates that 403 hyperscale data centres operating across the United States generated approximately 25.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, an amount comparable to Denmark’s annual emissions. The findings come amid growing concerns about the environmental consequences of artificial intelligence infrastructure, particularly the increasing dependence on fossil fuels to meet the electricity requirements of large-scale computing facilities. The research also raises questions about the transparency of technology companies’ environmental disclosures as governments worldwide compete to attract investment in AI infrastructure. The researchers estimated that the 403 hyperscale data centres consumed approximately 82 terawatt-hours of electricity during the study period, accounting for around 1.8% of total US electricity consumption. Depending on assumptions about how intensively the facilities operated, estimated electricity consumption ranged between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours. Associated carbon dioxide emissions ranged between 21 million and 31 million tonnes. The central emissions estimate was approximately three times higher than the level recorded in an earlier peer-reviewed assessment of data centre emissions in 2018. Hyperscale data centres are large computing facilities designed to support extensive cloud services, artificial intelligence applications and other digital operations. They house thousands of servers that require substantial electricity for processing information, storing data and maintaining cooling systems. Unlike conventional office buildings, these facilities operate continuously and require highly reliable electricity supplies. The increasing deployment of powerful graphics processing units for AI training and other computational tasks has further intensified their energy requirements. Importantly, the study does not attribute all electricity consumption to artificial intelligence alone. Hyperscale facilities also support conventional cloud computing, enterprise applications and other internet-based services. The study found that fossil fuels supplied approximately 54% of the electricity attributed to the hyperscale data centres examined. Natural gas remains an important source of electricity for these facilities, despite commitments by major technology companies to reduce emissions and expand renewable energy procurement. Researchers also identified significant geographical differences in electricity consumption and associated emissions. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa collectively accounted for more than half of the electricity consumed by the facilities included in the study. The environmental consequences of a data centre depend partly on the sources of electricity available in the region where it operates. A facility drawing power from a grid dominated by renewable or nuclear energy may generate substantially lower electricity-related emissions than a similar facility operating in a region heavily dependent on fossil fuels. The study estimated an average carbon intensity of approximately 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour for the facilities examined, compared with a national electricity generation average of approximately 348 grams. This suggests that although hyperscale data centres generate substantial emissions because of their enormous electricity requirements, their average electricity supply was not necessarily more carbon-intensive than the national grid. The findings arrive as electricity demand from data centres continues to increase worldwide. The International Energy Agency’s updated assessment projects that global data centre electricity consumption could rise from approximately 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030. Electricity consumption specifically associated with AI-focused facilities is projected to triple during this period. The expansion is creating challenges for electricity utilities, which must accommodate large industrial-scale customers while maintaining reliable and affordable power supplies for households and existing businesses. In the United States, opposition to new data centre projects has intensified over concerns about electricity prices, environmental impacts and the additional infrastructure required to support these facilities. Several candidates advocating stronger regulation or temporary restrictions on data centre construction secured victories in the November 3 midterm elections. The latest research also coincides with discussions at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, where governments and international organisations are examining ways to reduce the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. A voluntary clean AI initiative launched during the conference seeks to encourage greater use of clean energy, efficient electricity and water consumption, and improved environmental disclosures. The US experience is particularly relevant to India, where technology companies are expanding cloud infrastructure and investing in AI computing capacity. Large data centre projects can create employment, support digital services and strengthen domestic computing capabilities. However, they also require long-term access to electricity, cooling infrastructure and reliable transmission networks. For India, the challenge will be ensuring that additional computing demand does not undermine electricity affordability or wider environmental objectives. passages: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing infrastructure in the United States is generating carbon emissions comparable to those of an entire country, according to a new peer-reviewed study by researchers from Harvard University and other institutions.

Published on Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, the study estimates that 403 hyperscale data centres operating across the United States generated approximately 25.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, an amount comparable to Denmark’s annual emissions.

The findings come amid growing concerns about the environmental consequences of artificial intelligence infrastructure, particularly the increasing dependence on fossil fuels to meet the electricity requirements of large-scale computing facilities.
The research also raises questions about the transparency of technology companies’ environmental disclosures as governments worldwide compete to attract investment in AI infrastructure.

The researchers estimated that the 403 hyperscale data centres consumed approximately 82 terawatt-hours of electricity during the study period, accounting for around 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.

Depending on assumptions about how intensively the facilities operated, estimated electricity consumption ranged between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours. Associated carbon dioxide emissions ranged between 21 million and 31 million tonnes.
The central emissions estimate was approximately three times higher than the level recorded in an earlier peer-reviewed assessment of data centre emissions in 2018.

Hyperscale data centres are large computing facilities designed to support extensive cloud services, artificial intelligence applications and other digital operations. They house thousands of servers that require substantial electricity for processing information, storing data and maintaining cooling systems.
Unlike conventional office buildings, these facilities operate continuously and require highly reliable electricity supplies.
The increasing deployment of powerful graphics processing units for AI training and other computational tasks has further intensified their energy requirements.

Importantly, the study does not attribute all electricity consumption to artificial intelligence alone. Hyperscale facilities also support conventional cloud computing, enterprise applications and other internet-based services.
The study found that fossil fuels supplied approximately 54% of the electricity attributed to the hyperscale data centres examined.
Natural gas remains an important source of electricity for these facilities, despite commitments by major technology companies to reduce emissions and expand renewable energy procurement.
Researchers also identified significant geographical differences in electricity consumption and associated emissions.
Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa collectively accounted for more than half of the electricity consumed by the facilities included in the study.
The environmental consequences of a data centre depend partly on the sources of electricity available in the region where it operates.

A facility drawing power from a grid dominated by renewable or nuclear energy may generate substantially lower electricity-related emissions than a similar facility operating in a region heavily dependent on fossil fuels.

The study estimated an average carbon intensity of approximately 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour for the facilities examined, compared with a national electricity generation average of approximately 348 grams.

This suggests that although hyperscale data centres generate substantial emissions because of their enormous electricity requirements, their average electricity supply was not necessarily more carbon-intensive than the national grid.
The findings arrive as electricity demand from data centres continues to increase worldwide.
The International Energy Agency’s updated assessment projects that global data centre electricity consumption could rise from approximately 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030.
Electricity consumption specifically associated with AI-focused facilities is projected to triple during this period.

The expansion is creating challenges for electricity utilities, which must accommodate large industrial-scale customers while maintaining reliable and affordable power supplies for households and existing businesses.

In the United States, opposition to new data centre projects has intensified over concerns about electricity prices, environmental impacts and the additional infrastructure required to support these facilities.
Several candidates advocating stronger regulation or temporary restrictions on data centre construction secured victories in the November 3 midterm elections.

The latest research also coincides with discussions at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, where governments and international organisations are examining ways to reduce the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence.
A voluntary clean AI initiative launched during the conference seeks to encourage greater use of clean energy, efficient electricity and water consumption, and improved environmental disclosures.
The US experience is particularly relevant to India, where technology companies are expanding cloud infrastructure and investing in AI computing capacity.

Large data centre projects can create employment, support digital services and strengthen domestic computing capabilities. However, they also require long-term access to electricity, cooling infrastructure and reliable transmission networks.
For India, the challenge will be ensuring that additional computing demand does not undermine electricity affordability or wider environmental objectives.
The researchers acknowledge that their findings are based on estimated facility consumption rather than comprehensive public disclosures from individual operators.

As AI investment accelerates, the actual electricity requirements of the sector could already be considerably higher than those reflected in the study.

extraction.body: Artificial intelligence has developed rapidly in recent years, with tech companies investing billions of dollars in data centers to help train and run AI models. The expansion of data centers has raised questions on several fronts, including the effect these facilities may have on energy and the environment as the United States seeks an edge in the global AI race. In this analysis, we’ll take a closer look at data centers and what we know about their potential impact in these areas. This analysis explores the following questions: This analysis is primarily based on data from the “ Energy and AI ” report published by the International Energy Agency (IEA) in April 2025. Projected estimates on energy use at data centers are based on the IEA’s more conservative “base case” scenario, which assumes current industry forecasts and regulatory conditions persist. Data on the number and location of U.S. data centers comes from Data Center Map , an industry database designed to connect service providers and buyers. Counts are current as of Oct. 20, 2025, and include data centers that are planned, under development or currently operational. The database was created in 2007 and is based on information submitted voluntarily by operators, as well as other resources. Read more about the Data Center Map methodology . Information on the change in U.S. households’ average monthly electricity costs comes from the U.S. Energy Information Administration . This analysis also draws on news articles, industry briefings and a Center survey of 5,410 U.S. adults conducted Aug. 12-18, 2024. Here are the questions used for that survey , the topline and the survey methodology . Data centers are large buildings that house rows of computer servers, data storage systems and networking equipment, as well as the power and cooling systems that keep them running. This infrastructure is essential for companies that provide digital services. Whenever you send an email, stream your favorite TV show, save a family photo to “the cloud” or ask a chatbot a question, you’re interacting with a data center. While data centers have been around for decades , they’ve quickly expanded in recent years to support increasingly popular generative AI models. There are different broad types of data centers. Some common ones include: Hyperscale facilities typically host at least 5,000 servers, but many contain far more and have footprints measuring tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of square feet – with the largest hitting 1 million-plus. By comparison, the average data center usually has 2,000 to 5,000 servers. Smaller ones hold about 500 to 2,000. There is no federal registration requirement for data centers, so their estimated number varies depending on the source. Some owners of data centers also obscure their locations for security reasons and/or competitive advantage. One of the oldest and most comprehensive industry databases is Data Center Map , which estimates that the U.S. has over 4,000 data centers, including operational sites and those under development. A third of U.S. data centers are in just three states: Virginia (643), Texas (395) and California (319). Some of the nation’s key data center hubs are in northern Virginia, Dallas, Chicago and Phoenix. It’s likely they’ll retain their leading status: Half of the data centers currently being built in the U.S. are part of preexisting large clusters, according to an April report from the International Energy Agency (IEA). Companies choose data center locations based on a variety of factors, including the availability of capable power utilities, properly zoned land, and high-quality network access. This makes previously developed hubs ideal for further investment. More broadly, supporters see data centers as worthwhile to spur local and national economic growth and ensure national security amid the global AI race. Some also see opportunities for AI to help solve environmental problems and improve the health care industry , among other benefits. Total annual U.S. electricity consumption hit a record high in 2024 , and that ceiling could rise if data centers continue expanding at their current pace. U.S. data centers consumed 183 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, according to IEA estimates. That works out to more than 4% of the country’s total electricity consumption last year – and is roughly equivalent to the annual electricity demand of the entire nation of Pakistan. By 2030, this figure is projected to grow by 133% to 426 TWh. Because data centers handle many types of workloads, it’s difficult to distinguish the exact share of their total electricity demand that comes from AI alone. But a typical AI-focused hyperscaler annually consumes as much electricity as 100,000 households. The larger ones currently under construction are expected to use 20 times as much, the IEA predicts. Since data centers are often geographically concentrated, they can significantly strain the power grids . In 2023, data centers consumed about 26% of the total electricity supply in Virginia and significant shares of the supply in North Dakota (15%), Nebraska (12%), Iowa (11%) and Oregon (11%), according to the Electric Power Research Institute . Most of the electricity used by data centers – about 60% on average, the IEA reports – powers the servers that process and store digital information. This is especially true at AI-optimized hyperscale data centers, whose advanced servers are equipped with powerful computer chips that can perform trillions of mathematical calculations per second. These chips consume much more energy than their traditional counterparts, requiring two to four times as many watts to run. The next-largest component of energy use at data centers are the cooling systems that prevent servers from overheating. This share ranges from about 7% at efficient hyperscalers to over 30% at less efficient enterprise facilities. These cooling systems often require a large amount of water, though some types use more than others. In 2023, the country’s data centers directly consumed about 17 billion gallons of water – with hyperscale and colocation facilities using the lion’s share (84%) – according to estimates in a 2024 Berkeley Lab report commissioned by the U.S. Department of Energy. Hyperscale data centers alone are expected to consume between 16 billion and 33 billion gallons of water annually by 2028. (These figures exclude water consumed indirectly, such as in the process of electricity generation or semiconductor manufacturing.) As of 2024, natural gas supplied over 40% of electricity for U.S. data centers, according to the IEA . Renewables such as wind and solar supplied about 24% of electricity at data centers, while nuclear power supplied around 20% and coal around 15%. Natural gas is projected to continue supplying the largest share of energy at data centers through 2030, but nuclear power could eventually play a larger role. Several tech companies have recently announced purchasing agreements with nuclear power startups . Plans are also in the works to revive two retired nuclear power plants – Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania and Duane Arnold in Iowa – to meet growing energy demand from data centers. Several states – including California , Illinois , Minnesota , New Jersey and Virginia – have weighed bills requiring or incentivizing data centers to draw some of their power from renewable energy sources and to report their electricity and water usage . Lawmakers and utility companies have faced pressure in some states to protect residents from blackouts and higher electricity bills as U.S. data centers expand their footprint. Utilities often must make expensive upgrades to power grids so they can handle increased energy demands from new data centers. Smaller businesses and U.S. households often shoulder these costs unless ratepayer protections are put in place. For example, in the PJM electricity market stretching from Illinois to North Carolina, data centers accounted for an estimated $9.3 billion price increase in the 2025-26 “capacity market” (i.e., the total amount of electricity that providers in the region commit to supplying). As a result, the average residential bill is expected to rise by $18 a month in western Maryland and $16 a month in Ohio. Americans may see more widespread price hikes in coming years. One study from Carnegie Mellon University estimates that data centers and cryptocurrency mining could lead to an 8% increase in the average U.S. electricity bill by 2030, potentially exceeding 25% in the highest-demand markets of central and northern Virginia. Nationally, electricity rates have already risen for consumers in recent years, in part because utility companies have been replacing aging equipment to safeguard against extreme weather events and cyberattacks . For example, the typical U.S. household was billed $142 per month for electricity in 2024, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration . That’s up 25% from $114 per month in 2014. Pew Research Center has not surveyed Americans about the potential effects of data centers specifically. But when asked about the broader environmental impact that AI might have over the next 20 years, the public appears divided in its predictions, according to an August 2024 Center survey . A quarter of U.S. adults think AI will have a negative impact on the environment, while an identical share say it will have an equally positive and negative impact. Another 20% foresee a positive impact, while 30% aren’t sure. Rebecca Leppert is a writer/editor at Pew Research Center, focusing on religion . 901 E St. NW, Suite 300 Washington, DC 20004 USA (+1) 202-419-4300
