extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO. At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.” Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.” SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole. More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership.

The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
“We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia is beginning to have repercussions beyond the company's leadership transition. A robotics engineer who worked at the chipmaker has announced his resignation, saying the former CEO's vision and the workplace culture he helped establish were major reasons he wanted to remain with the company. Darrell Dai shared a lengthy post on X explaining his decision to leave Nvidia. While acknowledging that he did not have all the information surrounding the allegations against Huang, Dai said the lack of an explanation for the former CEO's departure had left him struggling to understand the company's direction and its treatment of employees. Dai recalled Huang's early commitment to CUDA, Nvidia's parallel computing platform, well before the deep learning boom transformed the technology industry. He also praised the former CEO for investing in artificial intelligence before it became a dominant industry priority and for backing the development of physical AI, robotics and open-source tools. However, Dai's post placed particular emphasis on the company's engineering culture, which he believed reflected Huang's leadership approach. “Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard. That is why this has been so disappointing." 'I nave not felt heard': Why the engineer decided to leave Dai said his admiration for Huang did not mean the former CEO should be exempt from scrutiny over the allegations. He also acknowledged that he did not know all the facts surrounding the controversy and could not prejudge the investigation. However, he said he found it difficult to accept Huang's departure without an explanation that helped him understand the decision. “I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny. What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me," Dai wrote. He also said the company's decision-making process had left employees feeling excluded, despite their contribution to building Nvidia. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected," he wrote. Dai acknowledged that some information could not be disclosed immediately but said employees were still being left outside a decision that had a direct bearing on the company and its future. He said Huang's vision and the engineering environment associated with his leadership had been central to his decision to work at Nvidia. With the former CEO gone, Dai decided it was time for him to move on as well. “I leave with sadness and gratitude," he wrote, thanking his colleagues and recalling the work they had undertaken together. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation from the tech company he co-founded in 1993 comes amid investigations by federal authorities and his own board of directors into allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, 63, had become a trusted ally of President Donald Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain. A timeline pieced together by ABC News indicates that Huang and Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang (no relation) have known each other since at least 2024, and that Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on the relationship by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. June 7, 2024 -- The first known photo of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang emerges of them sitting next to each other at Computex Taipei, the world's largest AI exhibition. May 22, 2025 -- Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are captured on video by Taiwanese news outlet TVBS leaving a restaurant together in Taipei. sources.title: Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it 'preposterous' - Fortune
passages: Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance.
That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world.
Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.
It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised.
“You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.”
Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years.
“The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2.
The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession.
The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that.

Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet , and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board.
On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote.
On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged.

Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”

Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts.
“This is preposterous,” says this interviewee.
“When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.”
Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities.
First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them.
Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board.
When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”
Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013.
According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L.
Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.
Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled.
The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge.
“They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person.
The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.
“That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven.
Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune , covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards. On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.” Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang. It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3. “You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.” It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven. For these observers, that failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, and a shocking disappointment for an enterprise that until now, seemed to be doing just about everything right. The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership. Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled. But that record so intoxicated investors that they didn’t install the safeguards that should have protected Nvidia should this ultimate “key man” depart in a crisis. “No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful,” says ex-CEO 1. “No one looked behind the curtain. Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts. “This is preposterous,” says this interviewee. “When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.” Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet , and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board. On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote. In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia’s largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley , T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%. Huang holds “just” 3.5%. Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board. “In any company that runs well over time,” says ex-CEO 2, “you’ll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives. When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.” Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years. “The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2. “When you have a CEO leave and everybody is asking what is the succession plan, the directors aren’t doing their job.” Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board’s first responsibility is preparing a successor: “It’s the most important thing the board does by a mile. The ground has to be plowed for succession. The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession. The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that. They should be making sure those candidates get the best roles to prepare them.” Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO’s reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement. But, the ex-CEO adds, “you’re moving people through different settings to see if they can grow, moving towards choosing the heir.” Hence, after a short interim period, a highly qualified candidate will ascend from a super-strong bench. Far more often, a permanent replacement stands in the wings, ready to take charge in the event the current CEO suddenly departs. Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities. First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them. Nvidia’s board failed on one of the two big items.” The leading consultant highlights the dangers of the Nvidia predicament. “The lesson from Nvidia is that emergencies happen more often than you think and it’s a big mistake to have a structure and mindset that assumes they won’t happen to you,” notes this person. “That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.” Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 “direct reports,” extolling the supposed virtues of a “flat” organization. What appears to be an extreme division of responsibility may account for the lack of a leader ready to lift the mantle from the legend. “It’s highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested,” notes ex-CEO 3. Adds ex-CEO 1, “In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12. The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn’t doing its job.” The issue also struck the consultant as a major negative. “The downside of having a very high number of direct reports is that none have been exposed to top roles in a deep and meaningful way. So it’s hard to imagine anyone internally who is ready to take over.” The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge. “They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person. Or, Nvidia could look outside. Ex-CEO 3 believes they’d go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s. “They’d want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something,” says this observer. passages: Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.

On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”

Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.

It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3. “You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven. For these observers, that failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, and a shocking disappointment for an enterprise that until now, seemed to be doing just about everything right.
The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.

Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled. But that record so intoxicated investors that they didn’t install the safeguards that should have protected Nvidia should this ultimate “key man” depart in a crisis.

“No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful,” says ex-CEO 1. “No one looked behind the curtain. Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts. “This is preposterous,” says this interviewee. “When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.”

Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet , and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board. On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote. In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia’s largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley , T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%. Huang holds “just” 3.5%.

Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board. “In any company that runs well over time,” says ex-CEO 2, “you’ll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives. When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”

Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years. “The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2. “When you have a CEO leave and everybody is asking what is the succession plan, the directors aren’t doing their job.” Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board’s first responsibility is preparing a successor: “It’s the most important thing the board does by a mile. The ground has to be plowed for succession. The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession. The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that. They should be making sure those candidates get the best roles to prepare them.”

Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO’s reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement. But, the ex-CEO adds, “you’re moving people through different settings to see if they can grow, moving towards choosing the heir.” Hence, after a short interim period, a highly qualified candidate will ascend from a super-strong bench. Far more often, a permanent replacement stands in the wings, ready to take charge in the event the current CEO suddenly departs.

Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities. First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them. Nvidia’s board failed on one of the two big items.”

The leading consultant highlights the dangers of the Nvidia predicament. “The lesson from Nvidia is that emergencies happen more often than you think and it’s a big mistake to have a structure and mindset that assumes they won’t happen to you,” notes this person. “That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 “direct reports,” extolling the supposed virtues of a “flat” organization. What appears to be an extreme division of responsibility may account for the lack of a leader ready to lift the mantle from the legend. “It’s highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested,” notes ex-CEO 3. Adds ex-CEO 1, “In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12. The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn’t doing its job.”

The issue also struck the consultant as a major negative. “The downside of having a very high number of direct reports is that none have been exposed to top roles in a deep and meaningful way. So it’s hard to imagine anyone internally who is ready to take over.”

The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge. “They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person. Or, Nvidia could look outside. Ex-CEO 3 believes they’d go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s. “They’d want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something,” says this observer.

Ex-CEO 2 concludes that the board was so excessively lax that, “If Nvidia hadn’t been performing well, it would have been exhibit A for an activist attack.” The fall of Jensen Huang unleashed another kind of broadside that exposed a big need for reform, and hopefully, it will have the same legacy as a raid from outsiders: A new era where this exceptional performer masters what it’s sorely lacking, and what most of the Fortune 500 already does far better: strong corporate governance.

coreStoryFacts.text: Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry.

Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.

So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.” SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA).
As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.
I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious.
He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority.
Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.
This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.
But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.
Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes.
Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly.
In a company this large, that connection matters.
It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.
I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation.
My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.
What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it.
What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.
I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here.
That gap has been more painful than I expected.
I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately.
But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.
Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.
Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay.
These are my personal views. — Darrell Dai (@darrell_dai) November 15, 2026

extraction.body: Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO. At the center of this theory is the reporting from The New York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based company, according to Bloomberg. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The New York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which says US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.” Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney said, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.” SemiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole. More than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia is beginning to have repercussions beyond the company's leadership transition. A robotics engineer who worked at the chipmaker has announced his resignation, saying the former CEO's vision and the workplace culture he helped establish were major reasons he wanted to remain with the company. Darrell Dai shared a lengthy post on X explaining his decision to leave Nvidia. While acknowledging that he did not have all the information surrounding the allegations against Huang, Dai said the lack of an explanation for the former CEO's departure had left him struggling to understand the company's direction and its treatment of employees. Dai recalled Huang's early commitment to CUDA, Nvidia's parallel computing platform, well before the deep learning boom transformed the technology industry. He also praised the former CEO for investing in artificial intelligence before it became a dominant industry priority and for backing the development of physical AI, robotics and open-source tools. However, Dai's post placed particular emphasis on the company's engineering culture, which he believed reflected Huang's leadership approach. “Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard. That is why this has been so disappointing." 'I nave not felt heard': Why the engineer decided to leave Dai said his admiration for Huang did not mean the former CEO should be exempt from scrutiny over the allegations. He also acknowledged that he did not know all the facts surrounding the controversy and could not prejudge the investigation. However, he said he found it difficult to accept Huang's departure without an explanation that helped him understand the decision. “I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny. What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me," Dai wrote. passages: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia is beginning to have repercussions beyond the company's leadership transition. A robotics engineer who worked at the chipmaker has announced his resignation, saying the former CEO's vision and the workplace culture he helped establish were major reasons he wanted to remain with the company.

Darrell Dai shared a lengthy post on X explaining his decision to leave Nvidia. While acknowledging that he did not have all the information surrounding the allegations against Huang, Dai said the lack of an explanation for the former CEO's departure had left him struggling to understand the company's direction and its treatment of employees.

Dai recalled Huang's early commitment to CUDA, Nvidia's parallel computing platform, well before the deep learning boom transformed the technology industry. He also praised the former CEO for investing in artificial intelligence before it became a dominant industry priority and for backing the development of physical AI, robotics and open-source tools.
However, Dai's post placed particular emphasis on the company's engineering culture, which he believed reflected Huang's leadership approach.

“Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation from the tech company he co-founded in 1993 comes amid investigations by federal authorities and his own board of directors into allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, 63, had become a trusted ally of President Donald Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain. A timeline pieced together by ABC News indicates that Huang and Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang (no relation) have known each other since at least 2024, and that Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on the relationship by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. June 7, 2024 -- The first known photo of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang emerges of them sitting next to each other at Computex Taipei, the world's largest AI exhibition. May 22, 2025 -- Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are captured on video by Taiwanese news outlet TVBS leaving a restaurant together in Taipei. Fall of 2025 -- Trump is briefed on U.S. intelligence that Jensen Huang is having an affair with a woman believed to be working for Chinese intelligence, a U.S. official and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News. The president does not take any action at the time, the official and sources said. Dec. 8, 2025 – Trump publicly announces a major policy change that would allow Nvidia to sell H200 AI chips to China in exchange for the U.S. receiving a 25% cut on the sales. Spring 2026 -- A classified memo is drafted that warns top administration officials that Jensen Huang has a close relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News, confirming reporting in The New York Times. May 12, 2026 -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio shares intelligence with President Trump on Air Force One showing Jensen Huang is in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter have told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the suspected espionage plot, sources with knowledge of the situation tell ABC News. Trump's briefing from Rubio, first reported in The New York Times, came shortly before Huang joined the president on a state visit to China, according to the U.S. official and sources. Huang was initially not listed among the CEOs joining Trump's China trip, but he joined the president's entourage in Alaska after news reports noted his absence. Trump later posted on his Truth Social platform that Huang was on Air Force One with him. Oct. 8, 2026 -- Huang attends the "Golden Age of American Innovation" summit at U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C., where Trump honors him with a National Medal for Science and Technology and Innovation. Oct. 29, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang and Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean tech company Megaspeed, had a "close relationship." Oct. 31, 2026 -- The Wall Street Journal reports that intelligence officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy. Nov. 8, 2026 -- Jensen Huang releases a memo to colleagues acknowledging "I was unfaithful to my wife." He goes on to say, "I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it." He also apologizes to his colleagues, the Nvidia board, partners and shareholders, saying, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility." Nvidia's board of directors announces it is launching an independent investigation into allegations that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board says that while it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information." Nov. 9, 2026 -- Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun tells reporters, "The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander." That same day, President Trump tells reporters he has spoken to Jensen Huang on the phone. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump says at a press briefing. sources.title: Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it 'preposterous' - Fortune
passages: Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance.
That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world.
Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.
It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised.
“You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.”
Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years.
“The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2.
The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession.
The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that.

Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet , and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board.
On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote.
On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged.

Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.”

Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts.
“This is preposterous,” says this interviewee.
“When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.”
Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities.
First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them.
Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board.
When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”
Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013.
According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L.
Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.
Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled.
The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge.
“They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person.
The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.
“That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven.
Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune , covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards. On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.” Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang. It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3. “You’ve got to ask why a tech company would go with a financial person.” It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven. For these observers, that failure is the ultimate sign of poor corporate governance, and a shocking disappointment for an enterprise that until now, seemed to be doing just about everything right. The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership. Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled. But that record so intoxicated investors that they didn’t install the safeguards that should have protected Nvidia should this ultimate “key man” depart in a crisis. “No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful,” says ex-CEO 1. “No one looked behind the curtain. Their success lulled people into a false sense of security.” This person notes that Huang’s obsession with occupying center stage, with casting himself as the leather-jacketed face of AI, and his otherwise slick salesmanship should have stirred doubts. “This is preposterous,” says this interviewee. “When you have a celebrity CEO, that person merits a closer look, especially when you have a leader who’s always putting on a show.” Unlike Elon Musk at SpaceX, Sergey Brin and Larry Page at Alphabet , and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms, Huang does not own a special class of supermajority stock that gives him control over the board. On the contrary, Nvidia has a single category of Class A shares that each carry one vote. In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia’s largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley , T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%. Huang holds “just” 3.5%. Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board. “In any company that runs well over time,” says ex-CEO 2, “you’ll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives. When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.” Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years. “The board wasn’t paying attention to how the company was run,” says ex-CEO 2. “When you have a CEO leave and everybody is asking what is the succession plan, the directors aren’t doing their job.” Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board’s first responsibility is preparing a successor: “It’s the most important thing the board does by a mile. The ground has to be plowed for succession. The board likes to talk about M&A and all these exotic things but they pale beside succession. The directors should be meeting regularly on the succession subject and talking about the best prospects at the next level, and level below that. They should be making sure those candidates get the best roles to prepare them.” Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO’s reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement. But, the ex-CEO adds, “you’re moving people through different settings to see if they can grow, moving towards choosing the heir.” Hence, after a short interim period, a highly qualified candidate will ascend from a super-strong bench. Far more often, a permanent replacement stands in the wings, ready to take charge in the event the current CEO suddenly departs. Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that “Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities. First, don’t do a deal that kills you, and second, have the right person running the place and a backup plan to replace them. Nvidia’s board failed on one of the two big items.” The leading consultant highlights the dangers of the Nvidia predicament. “The lesson from Nvidia is that emergencies happen more often than you think and it’s a big mistake to have a structure and mindset that assumes they won’t happen to you,” notes this person. “That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.” Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 “direct reports,” extolling the supposed virtues of a “flat” organization. What appears to be an extreme division of responsibility may account for the lack of a leader ready to lift the mantle from the legend. “It’s highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested,” notes ex-CEO 3. Adds ex-CEO 1, “In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12. The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn’t doing its job.” The issue also struck the consultant as a major negative. “The downside of having a very high number of direct reports is that none have been exposed to top roles in a deep and meaningful way. So it’s hard to imagine anyone internally who is ready to take over.” The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge. “They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person. Or, Nvidia could look outside. Ex-CEO 3 believes they’d go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s. “They’d want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something,” says this observer. Ex-CEO 2 concludes that the board was so excessively lax that, “If Nvidia hadn’t been performing well, it would have been exhibit A for an activist attack.” The fall of Jensen Huang unleashed another kind of broadside that exposed a big need for reform, and hopefully, it will have the same legacy as a raid from outsiders: A new era where this exceptional performer masters what it’s sorely lacking, and what most of the Fortune 500 already does far better: strong corporate governance. Despite this highly diverse, non-concentrated ownership, it appears that Huang totally controlled the board.
When you see a board that looks like a lot of old friends and people who’ve been there for decades, it flashes danger.”
Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013.
According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L.
Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.
Huang’s feat of hiking Nvidia’s valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled.
The consultant reckons that training an insider would prove a big challenge.
“They’d have to telescope the training to get the candidates up to speed in a hurry since it appears they haven’t been doing that and need to catch up,” says this person.
The sources identified four red flags warning that if its co-founder and America’s most celebrated tech CEO suddenly exited, Nvidia would face a stunning vacuum of leadership.
“That Nvidia has no obvious successor imposes a real cost.”

It astounds these sources that the world’s second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn’t have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven.

extraction.body: Just days after resigning, Jensen Huang is quietly weighing a way back into the top job at Nvidia. According to a new report by the Financial Times, Huang has talked with confidantes about returning as chief executive, even as allies in Silicon Valley push the company’s board to reinstate him. The resignation came after reports that Huang had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and with a subordinate. An independent probe by Nvidia’s board is still looking into the conduct behind what has become a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4tn chip company. One Huang ally told FT they are putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return, and will also try to win support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the ally said, adding that the effort has Huang’s support. A Campaign Gathers Steam Over the weekend, the push went public. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among the executives backing an open letter demanding that the board “Bring Jensen Back.” Several Nvidia employees have also gone public with their calls for his return and signed the letter, a sign that Huang still commands fierce loyalty inside the company. Two of Nvidia’s large shareholders have weighed in too. Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker wrote to the board on Friday, urging it to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” They pointed to the extraordinary success of his long leadership, and to the massive uncertainty surrounding his departure, as reasons for clemency. The Obstacles Ahead Still, the road back looks anything but smooth. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the company needs a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership after Huang’s departure, and the push is likely to meet resistance from key policymakers in Washington. Huang also lacks the controlling shareholding that other founder-CEOs hold, which means he cannot overrule the board. That board, along with a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress, is focused on steadying the company ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday. The FT reported on Friday that Arm CEO Rene Haas has been approached as a potential successor, though the board says no “formal” process has begun. The scandal has also put Nvidia’s compliance measures under deeper scrutiny, particularly around selling AI chips to customers in Asia with potential links to China. Even some of Huang’s supporters are unsure how to repair his reputation. As one person involved in the effort admitted, “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence.”

extraction.body: Just days after resigning, Jensen Huang is quietly weighing a way back into the top job at Nvidia. According to a new report by the Financial Times, Huang has talked with confidantes about returning as chief executive, even as allies in Silicon Valley push the company’s board to reinstate him. The resignation came after reports that Huang had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and with a subordinate. An independent probe by Nvidia’s board is still looking into the conduct behind what has become a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4tn chip company. One Huang ally told FT they are putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return, and will also try to win support from the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the ally said, adding that the effort has Huang’s support. A Campaign Gathers Steam Over the weekend, the push went public. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among the executives backing an open letter demanding that the board “Bring Jensen Back.” Several Nvidia employees have also gone public with their calls for his return and signed the letter, a sign that Huang still commands fierce loyalty inside the company. Two of Nvidia’s large shareholders have weighed in too. Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker wrote to the board on Friday, urging it to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” They pointed to the extraordinary success of his long leadership, and to the massive uncertainty surrounding his departure, as reasons for clemency. The Obstacles Ahead Still, the road back looks anything but smooth. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the company needs a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership after Huang’s departure, and the push is likely to meet resistance from key policymakers in Washington. Huang also lacks the controlling shareholding that other founder-CEOs hold, which means he cannot overrule the board. That board, along with a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress, is focused on steadying the company ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday. The FT reported on Friday that Arm CEO Rene Haas has been approached as a potential successor, though the board says no “formal” process has begun. The scandal has also put Nvidia’s compliance measures under deeper scrutiny, particularly around selling AI chips to customers in Asia with potential links to China. Even some of Huang’s supporters are unsure how to repair his reputation. As one person involved in the effort admitted, “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offence.”

extraction.body: The Commerce Department on Monday moved to close a loophole that has let Chinese companies lease Nvidia 's advanced computing power from data centers in third countries, effectively circumventing controls on sensitive chip technology being exported to China . The interim final rule from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is the first U.S. policy response to the scandal that led Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to resign last week after reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who worked for Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's biggest Asian customers. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release. The rule came after growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not doing enough to prevent possible diversion of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , in an interview on Friday with CNBC's "Squawk Box," blamed the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on its "entity list," which would restrict certain exports to it. Share prices of Nvidia and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence trade fell Monday morning after the interim rule was announced, among them chipmakers Micron Technology , Intel and Advanced Micro Devices . The rule is designed "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests," according to the text of the rule. The new restrictions "will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using" advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors produced by U.S. companies to train advanced AI models, the rule says. The rule also says that a license will now "be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs) – countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion." The New York Times reported on Nov. 9 that American authorities began investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed and one of its executives, Alice Huang, in 2024, "after the company started importing billions of dollars' worth of advanced Nvidia A.I. equipment into Malaysia." "Megaspeed had been planning and constructing data centers around Southeast Asia to serve Chinese clients, including Alibaba, the Chinese tech giant," The Times reported that day. "While that behavior is legal, U.S. officials were concerned that some of the Nvidia chips the company had bought were illegally routed into China." Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, and that she was a spy working for China. The two are not related. China's government has denied the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, as national security advisor, leads the National Security Council, warned President Donald Trump last spring that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, The Times has reported. Rep. John Mooelnaar, the Michigan Republican who is chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement on the new rule that it "sends a message to the Chinese Communist Party that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years." "Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy," Moolenaar said. "This new rule is an important step in keeping chips out of ill-intentioned hands, strengthens our national security laws, and will help protect America's lead in the AI race." Chris McGuire, a former deputy senior director for technology and national security at the National Security Council, in a post on X called the new rule "a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips." "The work here is not done, as there are some critical loopholes that remain open and need to be closed in a follow-up rule (namely those related to activities inside the United States)," wrote McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. "Commerce should move extremely quickly to close these. But this is the first time in over 18 months that the administration is starting to take export controls seriously, and does represent a meaningful step forward." McGuire said that the fact that the new rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the NSC "is remarkable and unprecedented." "I have never seen a BIS rule that was not written by BIS," he wrote. "That implies that Commerce was dragged kicking and screaming over the finish line by the White House and Treasury, and instructed to publish this rule rather than the rumored weaker one that it preferred. Remarkable." Commerce's new rule was published a day after Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state, the ranking Democrat on the Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, in a letter to Lutnick said that Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance have "used overseas data centers equipped with advanced Nvidia chips to train advanced AI models." "These companies are exploiting a loophole in U.S. export controls by using advanced American chips in foreign data centers even when those chips are restricted from the [People's Republic of China]," Cantwell wrote. "Despite warnings from the Bureau of Industry and Security that certain arrangements may violate existing restrictions, the Department of Commerce failed to close this loophole, allowing PRC companies to advance their AI capabilities using sensitive American technology," she wrote. The licensing trigger is a combined 12 million in aggregate total processing performance across a single facility or linked data centers. Indirect arrangements are also captured, including intermediaries that train, take part in training, or supply super intelligence models for restricted companies. Foreign data centers, chip exporters and foundries are now required to run customer due diligence to determine whether clients are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by entities in Macau or Country Group D:5, a step aimed at blocking circumvention through corporate restructuring or spinoffs. Facilities already serving restricted customers have 90 days from the effective date to secure licenses and keep those services running, or face future export restrictions. Applications will be reviewed case by case. Separately, BIS introduced destination-based licensing requirements for certain advanced semiconductor shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, citing elevated diversion risk. The agency said it would weigh the effectiveness of each destination's export-control regime and its coordination on enforcement when reviewing applications, and left room for the Commerce secretary to designate additional countries. Commerce will monitor jurisdictions that tolerate evasion and consider measures including import restrictions, while foreign persons involved could face Entity List designations or temporary export prohibitions. Qualifying commercial recommender systems are exempt, subject to reporting. The carve-out covers tools used exclusively to recommend products, services or content, such as those deployed by online retailers and social media platforms, but not systems that generate new content or embed AI models capable of doing so. The rule also tightens scrutiny at the manufacturing stage. Foundries and packaging houses that build advanced logic chips for designers based in China or other countries of concern can no longer submit paperwork or technical proofs to show the parts are destined for ordinary consumer electronics and therefore outside controls. Such chips are now treated as controlled by default, closing a route Chinese designers have used to tap overseas fabrication capacity. A further provision removes the de minimis exemption for advanced AI computing. Foreign manufacturers that embed restricted U.S. AI chips in servers built abroad can no longer rely on the argument that the finished product is mostly foreign-made; if they know the server is bound for a data center supplying large-scale AI computing to China or Macau, the sale is blocked even when only a small share of U.S. content is involved. The package also formally repeals the AI Diffusion Rule introduced in January of last year, which was never enforced and whose withdrawal was announced in May. Just before he left for his trip to China, President Trump told reporters he was not opposed to having former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company, and he was asked about the risks of their relationship. President Donald Trump: Jensen, as you know, wanted to sell to China. And the only thing he was able to sell to China were chips that were sort of obsolete, a little bit like our avionics, our aviation equipment. He wasn't allowed to sell them Blackwell or any of that, no. And I don't think you want to insult China just before you get there. Amna Nawaz: To help us sort through all of this, I'm joined now by Liza Tobin. She's the former China director for the National Security Council in the first Trump and Biden administrations and currently managing director at Garnaut Global. Liza, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for being with us. Amna Nawaz: So let's just look at that new rule that was issued this morning. Does it close the loopholes that it's intended to? Liza Tobin: Yes, this is a really important rule, and it's a long time coming. So, as you explained at the top, the U.S. and China are in a race to lead in AI.And the key variable there is compute, or these advanced AI chips that are primarily designed by Nvidia and made at TSMC in Taiwan. Up until recently, Blackwells were Nvidia's most advanced chips. And so for months and months, there has been this gap between what he said the policy was and what China was able to do remotely by accessing these chips kind of through the back door in these other countries. So, today, the Commerce Department closed that gap. And what's interesting is, of course, that there's kind of a disagreement playing out in public, where most of the president's Cabinet members, Secretary Bessent, the trade representative, Jamieson Greer, you had the director of national intelligence, Clayton, and many others who are all on one side clearly advising the president, you have to put out a rule. And the secretary of commerce, Howard Lutnick, was kind of the lone man left out who was wanting to keep this loophole open. Amna Nawaz: Liza, can I just underscore something here in terms of what made its way to China? Because we heard the president say there that the chips that made it to China were largely obsolete, that they did not put national security at risk, essentially. Liza Tobin: No, I think the president has probably gotten some bad briefings. We know that Jensen Huang for a long time had a lot of access to the president.

extraction.body: The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday published an interim final rule that for the first time puts remote access to American advanced computing power under export controls, extending Washington's reach from the physical shipment of chips to the question of who is allowed to log in and use them. The measure, written at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, targets companies headquartered in Macau or in Country Group D:5, the tier of destinations that includes China and is subject to a U.S. arms embargo. Under the rule, data centers anywhere in the world that provide covered computing capacity to such firms must obtain a license for the export, reexport or in-country transfer of the advanced chips involved. The licensing trigger is a combined 12 million in aggregate total processing performance across a single facility or linked data centers. Indirect arrangements are also captured, including intermediaries that train, take part in training, or supply super intelligence models for restricted companies. Foreign data centers, chip exporters and foundries are now required to run customer due diligence to determine whether clients are directly or indirectly owned or controlled by entities in Macau or Country Group D:5, a step aimed at blocking circumvention through corporate restructuring or spinoffs. Facilities already serving restricted customers have 90 days from the effective date to secure licenses and keep those services running, or face future export restrictions. Applications will be reviewed case by case. Separately, BIS introduced destination-based licensing requirements for certain advanced semiconductor shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, citing elevated diversion risk. The requirement does not amount to a ban: recipients headquartered in the United States, or whose ultimate parent is U.S.-headquartered, are excluded provided they meet specified reporting obligations. The agency said it would weigh the effectiveness of each destination's export-control regime and its coordination on enforcement when reviewing applications, and left room for the Commerce secretary to designate additional countries. Commerce will monitor jurisdictions that tolerate evasion and consider measures including import restrictions, while foreign persons involved could face Entity List designations or temporary export prohibitions. Qualifying commercial recommender systems are exempt, subject to reporting. passages: While H200 exports are now approved, heftier Blackwell-based chips remain firmly off limits, as will Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture.
It's remote access to this hardware that the Remote Access Security Act aims to curb.

In a statement, Chairman and cosponsor of the legislation, John Moolenaar, said, "The CCP’s AI ambitions are being fueled by its access to American chips housed in data centers located outside of China.
"This bill brings our laws into the digital age and makes it clear that cloud compute is subject to U.S. export control law, just like physical chips.
Closing these loopholes will strengthen U.S. national security and protect American innovation.”
The bill extends export controls on potent AI chips from the likes of AMD and Nvidia to cloud computing , a loophole that companies in China have allegedly used previously to access the hardware.
The fast-moving world of AI chip exports is a cat-and-mouse affair.

On the one hand, Washington continues to try to block Chinese access to its most potent AI hardware while also relaxing some restrictions, like allowing the sale of Nvidia H200 chips to approved customers .
Beijing's tack has shifted more towards encouraging the use of homegrown chips where possible.

So, whilst H200 export approval could be a boon to Nvidia, China has dragged its feet a little and still needs to approve H200 imports before big companies like the aforementioned Alibaba and ByteDance get the green light.
According to an investigation by the Wall Street Journal, INF Tech, a Shanghai-based startup , had allegedly gained access to 2,300 banned Nvidia AI GPUs by renting a server in Indonesia.
The 32 Nvidia GB200 servers were rented from an Indonesian telecommunications company in a deal thought to be worth $100 million.
Perhaps more concerning for U.S. lawmakers, the GPUs were allegedly bought after the company had secured the Chinese outfit as a customer.

The bill extends export controls on potent AI chips from the likes of AMD and Nvidia to cloud computing , a loophole that companies in China have allegedly used previously to access the hardware. As reported by The Information , the Select Committee on the CCP announced the passing of the Remote Access Security Act on Monday. The 32 Nvidia GB200 servers were rented from an Indonesian telecommunications company in a deal thought to be worth $100 million. Perhaps more concerning for U.S. lawmakers, the GPUs were allegedly bought after the company had secured the Chinese outfit as a customer. Similarly, both Alibaba and ByteDance were accused of training their respective Qwen and Doubao LLMs using Nvidia chips , accessed by renting data centers in Southeast Asia. The fast-moving world of AI chip exports is a cat-and-mouse affair. On the one hand, Washington continues to try to block Chinese access to its most potent AI hardware while also relaxing some restrictions, like allowing the sale of Nvidia H200 chips to approved customers . On the other hand, some Chinese companies continue to try to skirt export controls to obtain the best AI hardware available, both over the cloud and through physical means. Beijing's tack has shifted more towards encouraging the use of homegrown chips where possible. So, whilst H200 export approval could be a boon to Nvidia, China has dragged its feet a little and still needs to approve H200 imports before big companies like the aforementioned Alibaba and ByteDance get the green light. “The CCP’s AI ambitions are being fueled by its access to American chips housed in data centers located outside of China"
