A bipartisan bill passed by the U.S. House of Representatives aims to curb China's access to advanced AI chips by way of renting offshore data centers. The bill extends export controls on potent AI chips from the likes of AMD and Nvidia to cloud computing , a loophole that companies in China have allegedly used previously to access the hardware.

As reported by The Information , the Select Committee on the CCP announced the passing of the Remote Access Security Act on Monday. In a statement, the committee stated that the new bill "modernizes the Export Control Reform Act by expanding federal authority to restrict foreign adversaries’ ability to access technologies, including AI chips, remotely through cloud computing services."

In November of last year, multiple reports emerged claiming that Chinese companies were finding ways to access Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips by exploiting a cloud computing loophole. According to an investigation by the Wall Street Journal, INF Tech, a Shanghai-based startup , had allegedly gained access to 2,300 banned Nvidia AI GPUs by renting a server in Indonesia. The 32 Nvidia GB200 servers were rented from an Indonesian telecommunications company in a deal thought to be worth $100 million. Perhaps more concerning for U.S. lawmakers, the GPUs were allegedly bought after the company had secured the Chinese outfit as a customer.
Similarly, both Alibaba and ByteDance were accused of training their respective Qwen and Doubao LLMs using Nvidia chips , accessed by renting data centers in Southeast Asia.

The fast-moving world of AI chip exports is a cat-and-mouse affair. On the one hand, Washington continues to try to block Chinese access to its most potent AI hardware while also relaxing some restrictions, like allowing the sale of Nvidia H200 chips to approved customers . On the other hand, some Chinese companies continue to try to skirt export controls to obtain the best AI hardware available, both over the cloud and through physical means. Beijing's tack has shifted more towards encouraging the use of homegrown chips where possible. So, whilst H200 export approval could be a boon to Nvidia, China has dragged its feet a little and still needs to approve H200 imports before big companies like the aforementioned Alibaba and ByteDance get the green light.

While H200 exports are now approved, heftier Blackwell-based chips remain firmly off limits, as will Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture. It's remote access to this hardware that the Remote Access Security Act aims to curb. In a statement, Chairman and cosponsor of the legislation, John Moolenaar, said, "The CCP’s AI ambitions are being fueled by its access to American chips housed in data centers located outside of China. "This bill brings our laws into the digital age and makes it clear that cloud compute is subject to U.S. export control law, just like physical chips. Closing these loopholes will strengthen U.S. national security and protect American innovation.”

extraction.body: The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. Under the interim rule , the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries. The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others. The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries. “This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.” The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions. Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S. The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group. The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S. Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect. Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media. The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies. “By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.” Ram is a financial and tech reporter and editor. The bill extends export controls on potent AI chips from the likes of AMD and Nvidia to cloud computing , a loophole that companies in China have allegedly used previously to access the hardware. As reported by The Information , the Select Committee on the CCP announced the passing of the Remote Access Security Act on Monday. In a statement, the committee stated that the new bill "modernizes the Export Control Reform Act by expanding federal authority to restrict foreign adversaries’ ability to access technologies, including AI chips, remotely through cloud computing services." Beijing's tack has shifted more towards encouraging the use of homegrown chips where possible. “The CCP’s AI ambitions are being fueled by its access to American chips housed in data centers located outside of China"
a]:text-inherit [&>a]:underline"> When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

A bipartisan bill passed by the U.S. House of Representatives aims to curb China's access to advanced AI chips by way of renting offshore data centers. The bill extends export controls on potent AI chips from the likes of AMD and Nvidia to cloud computing , a loophole that companies in China have allegedly used previously to access the hardware.

As reported by The Information , the Select Committee on the CCP announced the passing of the Remote Access Security Act on Monday. In a statement, the committee stated that the new bill "modernizes the Export Control Reform Act by expanding federal authority to restrict foreign adversaries’ ability to access technologies, including AI chips, remotely through cloud computing services."

In November of last year, multiple reports emerged claiming that Chinese companies were finding ways to access Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips by exploiting a cloud computing loophole. According to an investigation by the Wall Street Journal, INF Tech, a Shanghai-based startup , had allegedly gained access to 2,300 banned Nvidia AI GPUs by renting a server in Indonesia. The 32 Nvidia GB200 servers were rented from an Indonesian telecommunications company in a deal thought to be worth $100 million. Perhaps more concerning for U.S. lawmakers, the GPUs were allegedly bought after the company had secured the Chinese outfit as a customer.
Similarly, both Alibaba and ByteDance were accused of training their respective Qwen and Doubao LLMs using Nvidia chips , accessed by renting data centers in Southeast Asia.

The fast-moving world of AI chip exports is a cat-and-mouse affair. On the one hand, Washington continues to try to block Chinese access to its most potent AI hardware while also relaxing some restrictions, like allowing the sale of Nvidia H200 chips to approved customers . On the other hand, some Chinese companies continue to try to skirt export controls to obtain the best AI hardware available, both over the cloud and through physical means. Beijing's tack has shifted more towards encouraging the use of homegrown chips where possible. So, whilst H200 export approval could be a boon to Nvidia, China has dragged its feet a little and still needs to approve H200 imports before big companies like the aforementioned Alibaba and ByteDance get the green light.

While H200 exports are now approved, heftier Blackwell-based chips remain firmly off limits, as will Nvidia's new Vera Rubin architecture. It's remote access to this hardware that the Remote Access Security Act aims to curb. In a statement, Chairman and cosponsor of the legislation, John Moolenaar, said, "The CCP’s AI ambitions are being fueled by its access to American chips housed in data centers located outside of China. "This bill brings our laws into the digital age and makes it clear that cloud compute is subject to U.S. export control law, just like physical chips. Closing these loopholes will strengthen U.S. national security and protect American innovation.”

sources.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
passages: The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers.

The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.

The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil.

The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil.

extraction.body: The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. Under the interim rule , the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries. The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others. The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries. “This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.” The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions. Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S. The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group. The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S. Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect. Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media. The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies. “By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.” Ram is a financial and tech reporter and editor. He covered North American and European M&A, equity, regulatory news and debt markets at Reuters and Acuris Global, and has also written about travel, tourism, entertainment and books. sources.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM
passages: OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools.

These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.
OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost.
The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.
ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning.
The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it.
It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.
In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers.

OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators.
It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.
OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children.
Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens.
Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children .

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens .

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.

OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.

What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.

OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children .

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens .

extraction.body: JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday. The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds. "There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved. Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET. A representative for U.S. Bank said that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan. The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers . — CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report. sources.title: Chase says software bug took down online banking and Zelle for thousands of customers
passages: Thousands of banking customers faced login troubles at multiple major U.S. financial institutions and payment platform Zelle on Monday following a technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase that sent shockwaves across the banking sector.

Bank representative confirmed that while its systems remained unaffected, "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle serves as the peer-to-peer payment platform utilized by America's largest banks, enabling customers to transfer funds to friends and relatives almost instantaneously.
"JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related ," said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
Chase was quick to clarify Monday that the disruptions weren't caused by a cyberattack , assuring customers that teams were actively working to restore full banking functionality.
"An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers," the spokesman said.
Monday's technical glitches appeared concentrated among Chase account holders and customers at other financial institutions attempting transactions with Chase.
An Early Warning Services representative confirmed the Zelle network maintained full functionality.
Evangelisti emphasized in his statement that the problem was confined to Chase's systems.
Certain Chase customers encountered a notification stating, "Some services aren't available.

coreStoryFacts.text: JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday.

The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds.
"There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC.
CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved.
— CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report.

Thousands of banking customers faced login troubles at multiple major U.S. financial institutions and payment platform Zelle on Monday following a technical glitch at JPMorgan Chase that sent shockwaves across the banking sector.

Bank representative confirmed that while its systems remained unaffected, "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle serves as the peer-to-peer payment platform utilized by America's largest banks, enabling customers to transfer funds to friends and relatives almost instantaneously.
"JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related ," said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
Chase was quick to clarify Monday that the disruptions weren't caused by a cyberattack , assuring customers that teams were actively working to restore full banking functionality.
"An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers," the spokesman said.
Monday's technical glitches appeared concentrated among Chase account holders and customers at other financial institutions attempting transactions with Chase.
An Early Warning Services representative confirmed the Zelle network maintained full functionality.
Evangelisti emphasized in his statement that the problem was confined to Chase's systems.
Certain Chase customers encountered a notification stating, "Some services aren't available.
JPMorgan Chase reported a technical issue on Monday causing delays in some customer transactions due to a software bug in their hardware systems.
JPMorgan Chase holds a market cap of $919.35 billion and a dividend yield of 1.91% as of Nov 17, 2026 05:04 WIB.
Other banks experienced delays in transactions involving Chase, particularly with Zelle payments, but were not directly impacted themselves.

extraction.body: JPMorgan Chase reported a "technical issue" that was affecting some consumer banking services Monday. The bank said a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" was causing some customer transactions to take longer than usual, though it said customers can still access their accounts and funds. "There is no evidence it is cyber-related," a JPMorgan spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," the spokesperson said. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." CNBC's Eamon Javers reported there was no indication of bad actors involved. Still, other major banks were listed in outage reports as transactions between Chase and other institutions appeared to get held up. Users reported errors as early as 11:30 a.m. ET. A representative for U.S. Bank said that company was "not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle is the peer-to-peer payments system backed by many of the largest U.S. banks, including JPMorgan. The outage reports come days after separate, widespread issues with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers . — CNBC's Leslie Picker contributed to this report. sources.title: Project Gutenberg brings free audiobooks to the global community with AI-generated book narration - Microsoft
passages: The collaboration between Project Gutenberg and Microsoft has increased the number of Project Gutenberg audiobooks with nearly 5,000 AI-generated audiobooks.

The oldest digital library and a leading distributor of free eBooks, Project Gutenberg wanted to make its collection more accessible to a broader community of members, including people who have visual impairments and those around the world who might not have access to traditional libraries.

A team from Microsoft approached Project Gutenberg about a collaboration to produce thousands of high-quality audiobooks using an AI-driven solution and then give them back to the Project Gutenberg community.
Microsoft donated much of the technology needed for the project, along with strategic planning to create a large collection of public-domain audiobooks.
In the future, Microsoft will also support Project Gutenberg to upgrade to Data Science in Microsoft Fabric , the SaaS version of machine learning in Azure Synapse Analytics, a PaaS product.
They’ll be able to regenerate files that are updated and expand the library to other books.”

“There’s a lot of demand for audiobooks, but we discovered we weren’t that good at making them,” says Newby.
Then, they parse the books and use SynapseML distributed ML library to create audio recordings using the neural text to speech capability in Azure AI services .
They can also generate human-like voices in other languages and adjust the voices to read with more emotion.

extraction.body: The oldest digital library and a leading distributor of free eBooks, Project Gutenberg wanted to make its collection more accessible to a broader community of members, including people who have visual impairments and those around the world who might not have access to traditional libraries. To achieve this goal, the organization collaborated with Microsoft on an AI-driven solution to create audiobooks at scale, creating nearly 5,000 new audio books. “Access to knowledge is a public good and a human right. And now, with audiobooks, Microsoft AI is helping us expand our reach to whole new audiences. Great literature is more accessible than ever.” Greg Newby, Director and CEO, Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation “Free access to literature creates better opportunities for people around the world,” says Greg Newby, Director and CEO of the Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation, which operates Project Gutenberg. sources.title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks
passages: Amazon-owned audiobook service Audible is turning to AI to help listeners find their next book.

The company on Monday launched a new “audio discovery” feature that provides a brief overview of a book’s themes and a summary of what readers liked about it, as well as commentary from an Audible editor or an author, in addition to playing the narrated sample.
These features have come as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, namely from Spotify, which introduced audiobook listening hours as part of its paid subscriptions.
That service expanded last month to over 180 markets.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend,” said Andy Tsao, Audible’s chief product and analytics officer, in a statement. “With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author.
Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily,” he added.

The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.
The overview audio itself is generated using AI, and the commentary is pulled from recordings of past Audible interviews, the company says.
Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.

The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.

The idea is that this type of expanded introduction to a story could help users decide what to listen to next, particularly when they’re on the go and don’t have time to scroll through comments or reviews.

Audible says the overviews will also draw on other publicly available materials, like synopses and metadata.

The feature will initially be available for select English-language titles in the U.S., and will arrive alongside new personalized collections based on users’ listening taste that could help them find other books.

extraction.body: The oldest digital library and a leading distributor of free eBooks, Project Gutenberg wanted to make its collection more accessible to a broader community of members, including people who have visual impairments and those around the world who might not have access to traditional libraries. To achieve this goal, the organization collaborated with Microsoft on an AI-driven solution to create audiobooks at scale, creating nearly 5,000 new audio books. “Access to knowledge is a public good and a human right. And now, with audiobooks, Microsoft AI is helping us expand our reach to whole new audiences. Great literature is more accessible than ever.” Greg Newby, Director and CEO, Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation “Free access to literature creates better opportunities for people around the world,” says Greg Newby, Director and CEO of the Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation, which operates Project Gutenberg. Created in 1971, Project Gutenberg is the oldest digital library and the first organization to make electronic versions of public-domain books available via the internet. It is also the leading distributor of free eBooks and publishes more than 70,000 eBooks on its website. A nonprofit organization, Project Gutenberg’s vision is to support freedom of information, giving people around the world access to great works of literature. “We believe everyone should be able to have a library, they should be able to carry it around with them wherever they go, and the works should be freely redistributable,” says Newby. “Our most popular downloads include some of the greatest literary works in history, from Pride and Prejudice to Dracula to Alice in Wonderland. ” As Project Gutenberg’s library continued to grow, its audiobook collection remained small despite the medium’s growing popularity—over the past decade, the share of US adults who listen to audiobooks has grown by more than 100 percent according to statistics reported on WordsRated.com. “There’s a lot of demand for audiobooks, but we discovered we weren’t that good at making them,” says Newby. “Creating high-quality recordings was beyond the capacity of our volunteer-driven team.” To make its collection more accessible to a broader community of members—including people who live in rural communities and don’t have access to a physical library, those with visual impairments, children who are learning to read, and those who prefer to listen to books—Project Gutenberg was interested in a scalable way to create audiobooks. A team from Microsoft approached Project Gutenberg about a collaboration to produce thousands of high-quality audiobooks using an AI-driven solution and then give them back to the Project Gutenberg community. These new audio recordings have made Project Gutenberg’s books more accessible to a wider audience of people around the world, including those facing accessibility challenges. Project Gutenberg first loads existing electronic books from its collection into Azure Synapse Analytics to allow working with large amounts of data. Then, they parse the books and use SynapseML distributed ML library to create audio recordings using the neural text to speech capability in Azure AI services . The capability turns the text of each book into audio using advanced human-like voices that can even convey emotion. “This is an AI innovation that reads text in a lifelike voice,” Newby explains. “The voices are trained to mimic humans in order to sound natural, and the result is convincing—a big upgrade over older versions of text to speech.” Some of the AI-generated audiobooks, such as recordings of Shakespeare’s plays, include different voices to portray various characters. They can also generate human-like voices in other languages and adjust the voices to read with more emotion. The generated audiobooks are saved as MP3 files to Azure Data Lake for distribution via the Project Gutenberg site and other podcast platforms such as LibriVox, the Internet Archive, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and Google Podcasts. The collaboration between Project Gutenberg and Microsoft has increased the number of Project Gutenberg audiobooks with nearly 5,000 AI-generated audiobooks. The project also will spread awareness of Project Gutenberg’s mission, improve their collection’s accessibility, and dramatically increase audiobook quality. Compared to traditional audiobook production using voice actors or volunteer readers, the AI-driven solution provides dramatic time savings. “When we learned about this neural text to speech technology, the possibilities were obvious,” Newby says. “It creates audiobooks en masse, reducing days of volunteer labor to just 30 seconds per book.” Microsoft donated much of the technology needed for the project, along with strategic planning to create a large collection of public-domain audiobooks. They’ll be able to regenerate files that are updated and expand the library to other books.” “Access to knowledge is a public good and a human right,” Newby says. “And now, with audiobooks, Microsoft AI is helping us expand our reach to whole new audiences. Our library is more accessible than ever.” Find out more about Project Gutenberg on Twitter and Facebook . “Free access to literature creates better opportunities for people around the world.” Greg Newby, Director and CEO, Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation Our mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.

sources.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
passages: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips.
Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said.
“I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”

Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.

passages: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday that he shares a “personal strong empathy” for ousted Nvidia leader Jensen Huang — but stopped short of saying Huang should return to the role.
During a Semafor event Monday, Altman — who was booted from his own AI giant in 2023 but reinstated just days later with a new company board — gushed that Huang has “long been a hero of mine.

Investors have been panicking that Nvidia’s dealmaking spree could slow without Huang at the helm — but Altman seemed to argue that the firm would survive just fine on its own, saying it’s “a behemoth of a company.”

Huang last week resigned as CEO, president and a member of Nvidia’s board after he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based business executive and suspected Communist spy of no relation — and reports later alleged he had at least two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
However, Nvidia’s embattled board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, sources told The Post on Monday.
In November 2023, Altman resigned from the top job at OpenAI in a shocking ouster after an internal review found he was “not consistently candid in his communications with the board.”

Despite a Washington Post report that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed President Trump on the spy plot, the president told reporters, “I haven’t heard that.” “I don’t know that she [Alice Huang] is a spy,” Trump said as he left the White House for a trip to the Philippines and China. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”

sources.title: ‘Heroes have flaws’: Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang - Semafor
passages: Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant.
Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return.
Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor.
Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage.

Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI.

In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout.

Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said.

extraction.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.” Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Billionaire Elon Musk has also backed a “Bring Jensen Back” petition online that has garnered more than 185,000 signatures. However, Nvidia’s embattled board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, sources told The Post on Monday. Investors have been panicking that Nvidia’s dealmaking spree could slow without Huang at the helm — but Altman seemed to argue that the firm would survive just fine on its own, saying it’s “a behemoth of a company.” The tech industry needs to take a “strong stance” on its long-term view of the future of AI, particularly after the Democratic midterm elections sweep, which was widely seen as a rebuke of AI and data center proposals, Altman added. Much of that backlash comes from people wanting to stay “in control of the future,” Altman said. “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future.” The public should feel confident that the people working on AI are “team human,” he continued. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said.

extraction.body: Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions. The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.” Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025. Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative. Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal. Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.” Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year. The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes. Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge. Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

The state of Querétaro is fast becoming famous for another thing: it is one of the Latin American hubs for the rapid expansion of the data center industry.
Most of these datas centers are in Colón or El Marqués, both municipalities near the regional capital, also called Querétaro.

Data from Cushman & Wakefield, a real estate firm, shows that, in 2023, the US and China were the countries in the world that used the most electricity to power data centers, as measured by megawatts capacity (1 megawatt, or MW, can power about 1,000 homes).
This same data also shows three Latin American cities among the global top 50 electricity usage by data centers.
At the heart of the construction campaign in Latin America is an industry wish list around deregulation and tax cuts and an unproven economic manifesto promising future prosperity.

These greater demands are driving a global expansion that makes comparatively less exploited regions like Latin America, a target for the biggest technology companies since many countries have vast natural resources, cheap energy and governments willing to lower taxes for these companies so as not to miss out on the future.
ISAGEN is in charge of six hydroelectric plants in Colombia, a country where most electricity comes from hydro power.
Ireland deploys the highest share of overall electricity production into data centers at 21% in 2024 –mainly by burning fossil fuels.

But they also have offices in the country, where they said that they had partnered with Brookfield Renewable Energy Partners “on a long-term renewable energy supply agreement to provide 100% renewable wind energy to the Clonee Data Center and Meta's Irish offices.”

Enel is an Italian multinational that is the electricity provider in many cities in various Latin American countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico and Panama.
Time and again this investigation found that promises of near-future solutions were being made to push through decisions that do not make sense in today’s technology and resource context.

While Brazil’s hydroelectric resources mean its grid is greener than most countries’, with 86% of the electricity coming from renewables and 64% from hydroelectric plants, climate change has affected rainfall, so energy production by thermoelectric plants has grown in recent years.

The nodes in this network are data centers, buildings stacked computers called servers that store reams of information from your personal details, to the images and texts that load when you doom scroll on social media or the encrypted data that allows you to bank online. These greater demands are driving a global expansion that makes comparatively less exploited regions like Latin America, a target for the biggest technology companies since many countries have vast natural resources, cheap energy and governments willing to lower taxes for these companies so as not to miss out on the future. It also includes actors from real estate, construction, energy and hardware. And this industry has been investing in strengthening its relations with national authorities, often influencing regulations that will later benefit them. Latin America, with its mix of fragile governance and resource riches is now witnessing what this unprecedented infrastructure campaign means at ground level. Data center companies argue that AI is the future of the economy , and that countries who refuse to embrace its potential will be left behind, missing out on tax revenue, jobs and services . Critics who warn that the industry consumes water and power at the expense of communities and the environment are told that AI will solve these problems in the near future as it advances sufficiently to develop new technologies. At the heart of the construction campaign in Latin America is an industry wish list around deregulation and tax cuts and an unproven economic manifesto promising future prosperity. For nine months a coalition of 17 newsrooms in 15 countries have used freedom of information laws, confidential sources and community reporting to capture how this wish list has been pursued and to test the promises made against the reality on the ground in Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, Mexico and Paraguay. The resulting investigation, “Big Tech’s Invisible Hand,” led by Brazil’s Agência Pública and El Centro Latinoamericano de Investigación Periodística (CLIP), found that promises of hundreds of thousands of direct and indirect jobs to be created are unfounded; economic benefits for local economies remain unproven; that industry claims of renewable energy disguise the deployment of new fossil fuel facilities to power data centers; and that multinational corporations’ complex structures deflect regulation and complicate efforts to monitor environmental impacts and resource consumption. Time and again this investigation found that promises of near-future solutions were being made to push through decisions that do not make sense in today’s technology and resource context. The energy consumption of AI is difficult to calculate , each individual query depends on various processes created previously, whose costs are difficult to individualize. the International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that a traditional Google search consumes 0.3 watt-hours. On the other hand, a ChatGPT query, on average, consumes 2.9 watt-hours. The IEA published a report in which it calculated that data centers consumed around 1.5% of all of global electricity production in 2024. This is equivalent to 415 terawatt-hours. The IEA said it expected this number to more than double by 2030, a forecast which other experts judged to be conservative. Ireland deploys the highest share of overall electricity production into data centers at 21% in 2024 –mainly by burning fossil fuels. This proportion led Irish authorities to restrict new data centers around the capital, Dublin, out of fear of creating blackouts. Data center companies claim they are solving this problem. Meta, which is one of the world’s main data center players, has five facilities in Ireland ( Data Center Map lists 133 data centers in this country). But they also have offices in the country, where they said that they had partnered with Brookfield Renewable Energy Partners “on a long-term renewable energy supply agreement to provide 100% renewable wind energy to the Clonee Data Center and Meta's Irish offices.” An accurate assessment of energy use by sector is prevented by the companies themselves who claim this information is an industrial secret. Data from Cushman & Wakefield, a real estate firm, shows that, in 2023, the US and China were the countries in the world that used the most electricity to power data centers, as measured by megawatts capacity (1 megawatt, or MW, can power about 1,000 homes). This same data also shows three Latin American cities among the global top 50 electricity usage by data centers. While an accurate picture remains obscured by secretive industry practices and incomplete public data, the pressure from some of the richest companies in the world to expand electricity production is intense. In 2024, Mexico’s Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) announced that it would increase Querétaro’s electrical grid capacity by 50%, citing the building of data centers in the region as one of the main drivers. The Commission announced a new power station, El Sauz II, which uses gas to generate electricity, adding more climate emissions. In an email sent to this investigation, Ascenty said: “The claim that the installation of new data centers in Querétaro, including those developed by Ascenty, would have motivated the construction of a new fossil fuel-powered plant is unfounded.” In an interview with N+, Arturo Bravo, General Manager of Ascenty Mexico (one of the data center companies in Querétaro), said his company finances part of the reinforcement work needed to cover the electricity demand of its data centers, that it is constantly talking to CFE and CENACE (the National Energy Control Center), and that its petitions for electricity demand are always accompanied by studies. While some data centers promise to use renewable energy—such as DataTrust in El Salvador which says it uses photovoltaic energy for its power, an assertion that has been impossible to verify— fossil fuel consumption keeps increasing. In the US, the rapid development of data centers is driving a surge in demand for electricity that the Trump administration intends to meet by burning more fossil fuels. The US AI Action Plan released in July and an Executive Order on “Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure" both seek to clear regulatory obstacles, including environmental protections. In last year’s environmental report , Google admitted that its greenhouse gas emissions have increased by 48% since 2019, mainly due to “increased data center energy consumption and supply chain emissions.” In the same report, Google said that “as we further integrate AI into our products, reducing emissions may be challenging due to increasing energy demands from the greater intensity of AI compute.” The company now assesses its much-vaunted net-zero goal in 2030 as “extremely ambitious.” Data center associations contacted by this investigation deny that the industry is looking to build more fossil fuel energy plants. Gutierrez, from ABES, in Brazil, said: “I don't see anyone building data centers wanting to encourage the use of thermoelectric, coal energy, diesel energy, which is more expensive.” In their written response, Digital Realty also said that their company “has a validated Science Based Target initiative (SBTi) to reduce Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions in accordance with climate science.” And that Digital Realty “has further committed to climate neutrality for its European operations by 2030 in accordance with the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact . In 2024, the company matched 75% of its global energy footprint with clean electricity, including 185 data centers matched with 100% clean power. Digital Realty has executed more than 1.5GW of renewable contracts to support our decarbonization efforts.” While Brazil’s hydroelectric resources mean its grid is greener than most countries’, with 86% of the electricity coming from renewables and 64% from hydroelectric plants, climate change has affected rainfall, so energy production by thermoelectric plants has grown in recent years. Tech Policy Press, the US partner in this investigation, asked environmental and consumer advocates how much information they could access on national data center projects. Most of them said it can be very difficult to get details, especially before the projects’ approval. This asymmetry is exacerbated by the widespread use of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) signed by data center companies and local governments. “It’s very difficult with the NDAs, prior to them actually being approved, to know what is going to be in the facility,” Julie Bolthouse, director of land use at the nonprofit Piedmont Environmental Council told Tech Policy Press. “We don’t know how much water they are going to use, we don’t know what kinds of emissions, and we don’t know how much electricity they will need or what type of service they will require,” she said. “So basically we gather information after the fact.” Free Press , a US nonprofit that monitors media and tech, has been tracking efforts to pass meaningful transparency laws. “A lot of companies release data in aggregate, which makes it difficult for folks in communities to understand what the specific impact will be,” said Jenna Ruddock, the organization’s advocacy director. “It’s important to pass those laws to make more information available earlier in the process, before the permitting and development is underway, when it is too late for the communities to have their say.” “We need to understand that cost and figure out how to deal with it in a way that doesn’t harm the places where [the data center] is going to be built,” she told Agência Pública. This investigation found that the relationship between technology companies and governments is complex and opaque. In some instances, governments desperate for foreign investment are working to attract data center companies, in others it’s the companies striving to convince governments and parliamentarians to let them build more facilities. In Chile the government, led by President Gabriel Boric, has been one of the most eager in the region to bring in these companies and it has enacted a national Data Center Plan called PDATA. Chile’s pitch is simple: the country is politically and economically stable, is committed to investing in technology and to facilitating investments in the sector, particularly by easing bureaucracy and weakening the environmental licensing process. PDATA, launched last December, includes clarifying regulations for data center companies. Some officials are not waiting to be lobbied. The Salvadoran government also approved new laws, including the Law for Innovation Promotion, the Law for AI Promotion and the General Law for the Digital Modernization of the State, which seek to turn the country into a tech hub. These laws offer tax benefits to data centers, in an effort to lure foreign investors. Direct investment in El Salvador has been falling in recent years. The Chamber of Commerce’s president Jorge Hasbún said it is due to judicial insecurity brought on by a seemingly permanent state of exception declared by the government. However, some companies have arrived. In 2021, Ronald Jiménez, then CEO of Codisa, the Costa Rican company that owned the DataTrust data center in El Salvador until it was bought by IFX Networks, said in an interview that his company had made its way to the country because “El Salvador is a magnet for investment attraction.” Energy companies, as well as real estate interests, are also driving the data center expansion. The AI boom is reversing years of declining power consumption and energy majors are among the interests stoking this speculation. Electricity companies stand to benefit from the construction of the new power stations that the industry is lobbying governments to finance in order to meet the demand created by the data centers that these same interests own. The DataTrust data center in El Salvador, for example, is owned by the company IFX Networks, which also owns data centers in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, and Honduras. IFX Networks is owned by another company, Ufinet, which in turn was bought by Enel Group, but then sold again in a transaction in which Enel retained a 19.5% stake. Enel is an Italian multinational that is the electricity provider in many cities in various Latin American countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico and Panama. Brookfield, which as mentioned owns a 49%-stake in Ascenty, and therefore in most of data centers in Latin America, also owns ISAGEN’s, a formerly publicly-owned Colombian electricity company, which it bought in 2016. ISAGEN is in charge of six hydroelectric plants in Colombia, a country where most electricity comes from hydro power. ISAGEN also operates other 21 electrical power stations in the country. The industry has enjoyed huge success in persuading governments across the world, and in Latin America, of the future benefits of AI infrastructure. Big Tech lobbyists, as in Brazil, are winning so often that they can complain about the rare carve outs that they did not receive. But the economic case for AI and in particular the hyperscalers’ approach to delivering unprecedented compute power, remains a “shot in the dark,” according to the Financial Times respected West Coast editor, Richard Waters. Elsewhere warning voices from villagers whose taps run dry, to communities facing rolling blackouts to workers whose pension funds are being bet on a data center-driven bonanza are either fed industry propaganda or ignored. Even if data centers do turn out to be more than another investment bubble, it is far from clear how the wealth created will benefit the countries who are surrendering a rapidly growing share of their national resources. This kind of one-sided wealth creation has clear echoes in Latin America for those willing to listen for them. “It’s just [data] storage and the exploitation of our natural resources.” Tania Rodríguez, leader of the Environmental and Communal Movement for Water and Territory (MOSACAT) told this investigation. Her group which emerged from the struggle against Google in Chile sees old forms of empire in the new technology: “It’s a new form of digital extractivism, we are being used by the Global North.”
