extraction.body: Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions. The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.” Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025. Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative. Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal. Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.” Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year. The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes. Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge. Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use. “Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.

extraction.body: The situation was so bad that the local government began to ration water with some families only getting access one day out of three. García cannot always wait for her share and makes the trek to her landlord’s house to fill jerry cans just to get by. While many residents of Colón make the connection between failing rains and dry taps, fewer are aware that they face a major new industrial competitor for their scant water resources. The state of Querétaro is fast becoming famous for another thing: it is one of the Latin American hubs for the rapid expansion of the data center industry. According to the Mexican Data Center Association , there are 14 facilities in the state. The local Development Secretary listed 19 permits responding to a public information request by our reporters. Most of these datas centers are in Colón or El Marqués, both municipalities near the regional capital, also called Querétaro. The cloud is a loaded image that evokes weightlessness and the idea that we are pulling down the digital services that many of us rely on from some ethereal space. But the reality of the cloud could scarcely be more grounded. Google Drive, OneDrive, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and others require gigantic physical infrastructure. The nodes in this network are data centers, buildings stacked computers called servers that store reams of information from your personal details, to the images and texts that load when you doom scroll on social media or the encrypted data that allows you to bank online. Data centers have existed for decades but the full implications of this industry are only now beginning to come into focus. Since the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, new, more complex, and more expensive AI data centers have been built, or are planned, across the globe. This new generation infrastructure requires generally more power and water than their earlier counterparts. These greater demands are driving a global expansion that makes comparatively less exploited regions like Latin America, a target for the biggest technology companies since many countries have vast natural resources, cheap energy and governments willing to lower taxes for these companies so as not to miss out on the future. The real-world industry that lies beneath the cloud is more than just the Big Tech titans in the US and its counterparts in China. It also includes actors from real estate, construction, energy and hardware. And this industry has been investing in strengthening its relations with national authorities, often influencing regulations that will later benefit them. Latin America, with its mix of fragile governance and resource riches is now witnessing what this unprecedented infrastructure campaign means at ground level. Data center companies argue that AI is the future of the economy , and that countries who refuse to embrace its potential will be left behind, missing out on tax revenue, jobs and services . Critics who warn that the industry consumes water and power at the expense of communities and the environment are told that AI will solve these problems in the near future as it advances sufficiently to develop new technologies. At the heart of the construction campaign in Latin America is an industry wish list around deregulation and tax cuts and an unproven economic manifesto promising future prosperity. For nine months a coalition of 17 newsrooms in 15 countries have used freedom of information laws, confidential sources and community reporting to capture how this wish list has been pursued and to test the promises made against the reality on the ground in Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, Mexico and Paraguay. extraction.body: Customers at several of the nation’s largest banks reported trouble accessing their online accounts Monday. Users reported issues with Bank of America, Chase, J.P. Bank, Wells Fargo and Zelle, according to Downdetector . A Chase spokesperson told The Associated Press the bank was dealing with a technical issue, not a cyber incident. JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” Joe Evangelisti, a spokesperson for the bank, said. Evangelisti said the problem is a "Chase-only" issue. This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us." The issue appears to be impacting Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, which include Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services. Bank spokesperson told the outlet its systems are not directly impacted but that "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays." Zelle is a "peer-to-peer" payment system that major U.S. banks use, allowing customers to send money to friends, family and others directly from their accounts. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. An Early Warning Services spokesperson said the Zelle network was fully operational. An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers," the statement read. The Associated Press reports that some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren’t available. Please try back later." An earlier statement by Chase on Monday read, "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.” The reports come days after a Microsoft 365 outage that began Thursday and disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for several hours. The company said the issue stemmed from an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a recent network change, adding the outage was not related to cyber activity or artificial intelligence. The FAA also ordered a nationwide ground stop Friday, temporarily pausing departures at U.S. airports for only the third time this century because of communications problems affecting air traffic control centers.

If it feels like the entire internet is in limbo right now — with major outages from Microsoft , JPMorgan Chase bank and United Airlines in the span of a few days — that’s because it is, cyber security experts say . And it’s probably going to get worse before it gets better. Major companies that underpin the entire digital economy are in a mad rush to update their complicated and often outdated computer systems as AI tools come online. There’s also a deadline to get this done before the holiday rush, when spending swells and more back-office employees take time off. “It’s holiday time, it’s travel time, it’s shopping. So you have all those higher spikes in volume, and more pressure to [update your systems ,]” Marva Bailer, CEO of tech advisory firm Qualaix, told The Post. Legacy systems are looking increasingly like Frankenstein’s monster, with bolted-on parts from AI companies and third-party vendors offering more points of failure, she said. That appears to be exactly what happened with Monday’s outage at Chase. The bank said a software bug within its systems caused a failure — but it also impacted related transactions with Zelle, Bank of America, Capital One, Wells Fargo, according to multiple reports. Also on Monday, United Airlines was forced to halt all departing flights thanks to a technical problem with its system. It came after Microsoft’s global outage on Thursday — which knocked out business software like Outlook email systems. The company said a “latent” software defect, combined with surging demand for servers, caused a cascade of failures. Then, on Friday the FAA ordered a nationwide ground-stop that left thousands stranded at airports. That has been blamed on a malfunctioning router in the middle of Arkansas that overloaded servers on the agency’s aging system. None of these incidents has been attributed to a cyber attack and the fears that AI could find and exploit new security flaws. But, AI could still be partly to blame, said Bailer. Along with the holidays. Companies often freeze software changes during major shopping events such as Black Friday, creating a deadline for completing upgrades. The FAA and airlines would be under similar pressure as travelers prepare to crisscross the nation en masse. Meanwhile, AI is allowing companies to identify software vulnerabilities at a much faster clip — potentially leaving IT workers with more problems to fix. Complicating matters is an army of behind-the-scenes middlemen that most Americans don’t see, but rely on every time they swipe a debit card, book a flight, or send a payment. These third-party tech giants provide much of the technological muscle behind the banking industry. “They do the billing. They do the encryption. They actually move the money,” Bailer said. “We’ve added layers,” she added. “When we think about a banking system in layers, we think about branches and ATMs, but do we really think about Zelle?” A faulty software patch or security update could potentially prevent otherwise functioning computer systems from communicating with one another — grinding the gears across the industry. And the consequences of another meltdown during the holiday shopping frenzy could be particularly devastating for retailers. “It’s not just consumers,” Bailer said. “It’s small businesses.” Chase has not disclosed whether a software update triggered Monday’s outage. There is no evidence that the three incidents were connected or that AI was responsible. With Post wires.

REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Nov 16 (Reuters) - JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Monday it experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug, adding that the issue may have affected other banks receiving its slowed transactions. "JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence it is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a spokesperson for the bank said. Customers can still access accounts and funds, and the bank is working hard to resolve the issue, the spokesperson added. "This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us." The incident follows several other recent problems that have put users on edge, including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week, and Microsoft's global email outage, while last month crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack. User reports on Monday also indicated problems at Bank of America, US Bank and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com . A US Bank spokesperson said its systems were not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the US Bank spokesperson added. Nov 16 (Reuters) - JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Monday it experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug, adding that the issue may have affected other banks receiving its slowed transactions.

"JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence it is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," a spokesperson for the bank said.

Customers can still access accounts and funds, and the bank is working hard to resolve the issue, the spokesperson added. "This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us."

The incident follows several other recent problems that have put users on edge, including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week, and Microsoft's global email outage, while last month crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack.
User reports on Monday also indicated problems at Bank of America, US Bank and Wells Fargo, according to Downdetector.com .

A US Bank spokesperson said its systems were not directly impacted. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the US Bank spokesperson added.

(Reporting by Anna Peverieri in Barcelona and Pritam Biswas in Bengaluru; Additional reporting by Disha Mishra, Nupur Anand and Saeed Azhar; Editing by Michelle Price, Tasim Zahid and Jonathan Spicer )

extraction.body: Some customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their ATM cards or complete transactions JPMORGAN Chase, the United States’ largest bank, reported trouble processing transactions on Monday (Nov 16), and said that the technical issues it was experiencing might have caused problems for customers of other banks. “JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank said in a statement, adding that there was no evidence that the problem was “cyber-related.” “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” the bank added. “This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The banking issues were reported days after a global outage at Microsoft disrupted communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to fail, officials said. There was no indication that the disruptions had any common cause. But together, they added to a sense of gloom in social media chatter about troubles with modern technology. “Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week,” Mike Chapple, a professor of information technology, analytics and operations at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement. “When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day.” JPMorgan Chase, which serves more than 86 million customers at 5,000 Chase Bank branches across the United States, said its customers “still have access to their accounts and funds.” “We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today,” it said. Some Chase Bank customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their ATM cards or complete transactions at branches on Monday. Customers at several other major banks, including Wells Fargo, US Bank and Bank of America, also reported problems on Monday, according to Downdetector.com, a website that tracks user reports of outages. Users also reported issues with the online payment platform Zelle. US Bank said in a statement that its systems had not been “directly impacted.” “However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” it said. “Zelle is operating as it should,” it said in a statement, which noted that customers who use the platform may be having trouble because of problems at their own banks. “An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” it said. Wells Fargo and Bank of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Microsoft outage , which started on Thursday and was resolved on Saturday, affected some of its most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot. Microsoft said the outage had been caused by a “technical issue” and not a cyberattack or AI agent. The FAA ground stop, which was lifted hours after it was issued on Friday, created a cascade of flight delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend. Beyond Chase, users reported transaction issues at Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Bank of America, and the online payment service Zelle. However, it has not been confirmed that the service failures at these financial institutions were caused by the same issue as Chase. U.S. Bank stated that its own systems were not directly affected. However, it explained that customers sending or receiving money through Zelle via other financial institutions might experience transaction delays. Zelle also stated that while its own service is operating normally, issues at individual financial institutions could affect payments for some customers. This computing disruption occurred immediately after the Microsoft service outage and the flight delays and cancellations following the Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop order. Recently, there have been a series of failures in systems that rely on large-scale services across the financial, technology, and transportation sectors in the U.S. Chase, Microsoft, and the Federal Aviation Administration have not presented any signs of cyberattacks in relation to their respective incidents. As the transaction delays caused by the Chase failure spread to remittance services through other financial institutions, the impact of interconnected structures among financial institutions on user services was revealed. extraction.body: On the 16th (local time), a computer glitch caused delays in transaction processing at JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank in the U.S. Chase stated that the cause was a software bug in its on-premise hardware system and that there was no evidence of a cyberattack. While some customers were able to access their accounts and funds, transaction processing took longer than usual. Users also reported inconveniences such as being unable to use cards at automated teller machines (ATMs) and experiencing delays in branch services. The bank stated that this issue was not a total system failure. It added that other financial institutions that transact with Chase could also be affected by the processing delays and that it would carry out restoration work within the 16th. As of the 17th, no separate official announcement has been made stating that services have returned to normal. JPMorgan Chase identified the cause of the failure as a software bug in its on-premise hardware system. It maintains that there are no signs of external intrusion or evidence of a cyberattack. Chase operates approximately 5,000 branches across the U.S. and has over 86 million customers. As an error occurred in a system that processes large-scale financial transactions, inconveniences appeared not only in online services but also in ATM and branch operations. Beyond Chase, users reported transaction issues at Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Bank of America, and the online payment service Zelle. However, it has not been confirmed that the service failures at these financial institutions were caused by the same issue as Chase. U.S. Bank stated that its own systems were not directly affected. However, it explained that customers sending or receiving money through Zelle via other financial institutions might experience transaction delays. Zelle also stated that while its own service is operating normally, issues at individual financial institutions could affect payments for some customers. This computing disruption occurred immediately after the Microsoft service outage and the flight delays and cancellations following the Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop order. Recently, there have been a series of failures in systems that rely on large-scale services across the financial, technology, and transportation sectors in the U.S. Chase, Microsoft, and the Federal Aviation Administration have not presented any signs of cyberattacks in relation to their respective incidents. As the transaction delays caused by the Chase failure spread to remittance services through other financial institutions, the impact of interconnected structures among financial institutions on user services was revealed. Tom Lee, the longtime Wall Street bull and Fundstrat Global Advisors head of research, says a new "crypto spring" may be underway, linking renewed strength in digital assets to the same AI-driven optimism fueling US equities. Lee's latest remarks come as Bitcoin trends higher and investor sentiment toward risk assets improves, with the strategist also predicting that 2027 could deliver "one of the biggest rallies we see in our lifetime." On Wednesday, Lee's bullish comment came in response to veteran technical analyst John Bollinger, creator of the widely followed Bollinger Bands indicator, who said Bitcoin's trend had turned positive. "Yesterday our trend model for Bitcoin turned positive, and we took a position in our Tactica program, which is now fully invested," Bollinger wrote on X. Lee, who has a long history of optimistic Bitcoin predictions, shared the post with the caption: "Crypto spring is here." His latest endorsement arrives as crypto markets attempt to regain momentum after months of volatility. At the time of reporting, Bitcoin's price was trading at around $81,079, up almost 20% over the past month. However, a small 2% pullback in the last 24 hours reflects a pause after a recent rally, analysts said, driven by institutional profit-taking and a failed technical breakout. Speaking on CNBC on Wednesday, Lee tied the crypto optimism to what he described as a broader bullish backdrop for equities, driven by AI-related demand and semiconductor scarcity. "Stocks are rising for the right reasons," Lee said, pointing to strong corporate earnings. He added that semiconductor stocks still do not appear excessively valued despite recent gains. "The forward P/E of the semi index is still only 22 times," Lee said. Adding: "They've gotten as high as 35 times over the last 20 years. So to me, there's still pretty good risk reward." Lee also said large amounts of capital remain on the sidelines despite the recent rally. "There was so much skepticism as the war started and reached its crescendo that we do believe there's still a lot of money on the sidelines," he said. He added that retail investors may now be driving some of the sharp moves in semiconductor and memory-related stocks. At the center of Lee's thesis is the belief that AI could materially boost US economic growth without reigniting inflation pressures. "One of the recurring themes is that AI for the US is probably adding two percentage points to GDP each year for the next five years," Lee said from the Milken Institute Global Conference. "That is like 6% S&P earnings growth coming from AI productivity." Still, he argued the long-term setup remains constructive. "AI and the scarcity — and the US is the provider of that scarcity — is why I think we can exit 7700 or higher," Lee said. He added that "maybe 2027 is one of the biggest rallies we see in our lifetime." Lee's bullish stance has drawn renewed attention after several high-profile stock market calls proved directionally accurate, despite several missed crypto outlooks. In 2023, he was among the few major strategists forecasting a strong rally in the S&P 500 while many on Wall Street expected a recession-driven decline. His year-end target of 4,750 came close to the benchmark's actual close of 4,769. Critics have frequently labeled him a "perma-bull," noting that he has repeatedly issued aggressive Bitcoin forecasts that failed to materialize. In January, Lee said he expected Bitcoin to reach a new all-time high this year and potentially surge to $250,000. "We think Bitcoin will make a new high this year," Lee said on the Master Investor podcast. "If Bitcoin makes a new all-time high, we know that that deleveraging event is behind us." Lee reiterated his longstanding view of Bitcoin as "digital gold," while acknowledging that cryptocurrency ownership still lags behind that of traditional precious metals among investors. "More people own gold than own crypto," Lee said. "But the path to getting that adoption rate higher is going to be very jagged." passages: Sam Daodu is a crypto analyst and the editor of 24/7 Wall St.'s Crypto Desk, where he covers Bitcoin, XRP, Ethereum, Solana and the altcoins investors search for most.
His work focuses on price levels, spot ETF flows, on-chain data and the regulatory decisions that move crypto markets, written so a first-time buyer and a seasoned trader can both use it.
Sam has written about crypto professionally since 2019 and has published more than 2,000 articles.
His analysis is syndicated on Yahoo Finance, MSN and AOL and has been cited by other crypto news sites.
He also founded MacLabs Marketing, a content and personal branding agency for crypto founders and executives.
When he isn't reading charts, Sam is usually at the gym or watching One Piece, a series he maintains has better tokenomics than most altcoins.
Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at about $64,946, down 26% this year and 48.5% from its all-time high of $126,080 reached on October 6, 2025.
The recent downturn has been significant, plummeting from an $84,082 close on October 21 to a low close of $64,120 on November 14.
So how do Wall Street’s Bitcoin price predictions for 2027 hold up after the crash?
Predictions for Bitcoin’s price in 2027 vary significantly among four major firms.
Citigroup ( NYSE:C ) sets the lowest target at $113,000, while Bernstein, Siebert Financial ( NASDAQ:SIEB ) and Galaxy Digital ( NASDAQ:GLXY ) set targets between $150,000 and $250,000.
All of these predictions were made before the sharp decline in November and remain unchanged.
Given these factors, our year-end Bitcoin price prediction sees a likely December 31 close between $65,000 and $73,000.
Citi’s forecast requires Bitcoin to rise about 74%, while Bernstein’s needs Bitcoin to more than double.
Galaxy Digital's Alex Thorn still stands by a sky-high call, yet ETF money is leaving and corporate buyers are turning into sellers.
Which price level decides whether Bitcoin's 2027 forecast is a bold bet…
At this stage, only Citi’s $113,000 target appears realistic, though it would require positive flows into Bitcoin ETFs.
So those three look unlikely by the end of 2027, and our look at what one Bitcoin could be worth in 2030 takes a longer view.
Wall Street analysts are calling for Bitcoin to nearly double in 15 weeks, but traders putting real money on the line disagree sharply.
The gap between institutional forecasts and prediction market odds reveals a…
Citigroup just issued a bold new Bitcoin price target based on surprisingly modest assumptions, but its own track record in 2026 reveals how quickly that forecast could collapse.
Bernstein ties its prediction to Bitcoin’s four-year cycle, in which the halving, a scheduled reduction in new Bitcoin issuance, tends to come before market peaks.

“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”

“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”

Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.

The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.

Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

sources.title: California sues OpenAI, alleges it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
passages: Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release.

The company called the Hugging Face attack "evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed." Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta's office said.
California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology.

An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined.

They went on to say that "AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions." They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws.
On Monday, his office said such attacks "may just be the tip of the iceberg," but the scope of the problem isn't fully known because OpenAI hasn't answered "detailed questions" about them.
“This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated,” OpenAI said in a statement.

The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections.
OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly.
California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors.

extraction.body: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips. On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.” The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold. In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe. Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions. Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.) Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations. Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted. Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.” “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.” There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.” At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.” “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.” However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported . China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions. However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.” Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated. “Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.” The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said. Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. passages: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips.

On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”

At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”
“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”
However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported .
China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.
However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”

Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”

The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”

extraction.body: Trump bets China won’t mind US blocking remote access to AI chips. On the heels of the Nvidia scandal , the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training. In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.” The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold. In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.” Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported . Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe. Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions. Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.) Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations. Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted. Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.” “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.” There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.” At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.” “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.” However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported . China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions. However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.” Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated. “Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.” The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said. Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”

The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported .

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy . Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”

At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”
“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”
However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported .
China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.
However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”

Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”

The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”

extraction.body: Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. sources.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
passages: After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks.
But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses.
Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models.
But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor.
That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems.
Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities.

Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold.
From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally.
The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.
Where was Nvidia’s security team? Connie Loizos

In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.

Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.

Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.

The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.

Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.

A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.

It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online , which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
